documents.abstract: Title Anatomical target and guidance technique for cervical medial branch block: a systematic review and meta-analysis of targeting accuracy and diagnostic yield 1、Registration status This registration is submitted retrospectively. Protocol development began before the searches reported below were executed. At the time of registration on 15 October 2026, the following activities had already been completed: database searching (Europe PMC, OpenAlex, VIP, ClinicalTrials.gov), title and abstract screening, full-text retrieval for 62 records, data extraction from the included cohorts, and the primary meta-analysis. Registration was delayed because the review was initiated as an internal evidence synthesis and the decision to prepare it for publication was made only after the analyses had been run. A later registration cannot establish that the methodological decisions were pre-specified. 2、Background Neck pain is among the most prevalent musculoskeletal complaints worldwide. A substantial proportion of cases arise from the cervical zygapophysial (facet) joints, with controlled diagnostic studies estimating a prevalence of 36% to 67%. Because clinical examination cannot reliably identify this source, diagnosis depends on image-guided blockade of the medial branch nerves. The technical elements of the procedure (anatomical target, guidance modality, confirmatory tool, and injectate volume) are inconsistently defined, and their influence on targeting accuracy, block positivity, and safety has not been synthesised. 3、Review question In adults with chronic neck pain or cervicogenic headache of suspected cervical facet joint origin, how do anatomical target definitions and guidance or confirmation techniques for cervical medial branch block affect targeting accuracy, block diagnostic yield, and safety? 4、Eligibility criteria Included: original studies of any design (randomised trials, prospective and retrospective cohorts, cross-sectional studies, diagnostic accuracy studies, case series with at least five participants); adults aged 18 years or older with chronic neck pain and/or cervicogenic headache undergoing cervical medial branch block or facet joint block; studies reporting block-level outcomes (targeting accuracy, technical success, block positivity rate, or comparisons of target definitions, guidance modalities, or patient-selection strategies); cadaveric and anatomical studies reporting human target accuracy (analysed separately); publication from 2015 onwards. Excluded: studies reporting only post-radiofrequency outcomes without block-level data; systematic reviews, narrative reviews, study protocols, editorials, and case reports; studies of the thoracic, lumbar, or sacral regions; studies without extractable quantitative data. 5、Outcomes Primary: proportion of patients achieving at least 50% pain relief after cervical medial branch block or radiofrequency procedures, at three months or later. Secondary: technical success and targeting accuracy according to the definition used by each study; block positivity rate at thresholds of 50% and 80% relief; complications and adverse events, including intravascular injection; false-positive and false-negative rates against subsequent radiofrequency outcome. 6、Search strategy Searched resources: Europe PMC (indexing MEDLINE/PubMed), OpenAlex, VIP, and the ClinicalTrials.gov registry; reference lists and citations of included studies and relevant previous reviews were screened. Search period 2015 onwards. Search terms combined population terms (cervical, neck pain, cervicogenic, whiplash, cervical facet) with intervention terms (medial branch, facet joint block, facet block, zygapophysial). Resources not searched: Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, ProQuest, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL, Wanfang, SinoMed, and the WHO ICTRP registry could not be searched because the subscription proxy service used for these resources was non-functional throughout the review period. OpenAlex was used as an additional bibliographic index to partially compensate; it is not equivalent to a curated citation database. 7、Study selection and data extraction Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened against the eligibility criteria by one investigator and an AI-assisted screening tool independently, with disagreements resolved by discussion. A calibration exercise on 25 records preceded formal screening (human-AI agreement 81.8%, kappa 0.58). Data were extracted with a standardised form covering study identifiers, design, population, cervical levels, target definition, guidance modality, needle approach, confirmatory tool, injectate and volume, and outcome definitions with numerators and denominators. All values were verified against source full texts. 8、Risk of bias and certainty of evidence Risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies, RoB 2 for randomised trials, and QUADAS-2 or a study-specific checklist for diagnostic accuracy and cadaveric studies. Certainty of evidence was assessed with GRADE, starting at low for observational designs. 9、Data synthesis Proportions were pooled using a random-intercepts logistic model with logit transformation, maximum likelihood estimation of tau-squared, and the Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Heterogeneity was quantified with tau-squared, I-squared, and Cochran Q. Pre-specified subgroup analyses compared radiofrequency versus block procedures, guidance modality, injectate volume, confirmatory tool, and follow-up duration. Leave-one-out analysis was performed for the primary outcome and the subgroup comparison. Publication bias was not assessed because of the small number of studies per outcome. Safety outcomes were summarised descriptively rather than pooled, because of extreme imbalance in study size across cohorts. Analyses used R 4.6.1 with the meta package. 10、Expected outcomes / dissemination The review will quantify the proportion of patients achieving meaningful pain relief after cervical medial branch procedures, describe technical success according to the definition used, and summarise the safety profile. It will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal (target: Medicine (Baltimore)). The registration number and DOI will be cited in the final article.

With the advent of Covid-19, it is necessary to repurpose new treatment alternatives, either in the form of an effective single dose of these antidiabetic drug agents or an efficacious combination of them for elderly population with or had suffered this condition. Newer medication classes for diabetes have been increasing in use, and their utilization varied across provinces and how the COVID-19 pandemic may have affected these trends. This mini review has the objective of predicting the targets of bioactive small molecules in human using healthcare applied artificial intelligence. These substances in the body are target specific receptors on the surface of cells, and antidiabetic drugs contains moiety´s and functional groups that may act on one or several subtypes of receptors. The tool is a tuned algorithm, with novel data bank in web interface. Information figures of Swiss Target Prediction (STP), which allow predictions on therapy combinations and probable side effects, were reordered. The bibliographic databases were searched to identify existing cost studies, economic evaluations and models, and most of the parameters were derived from the published literatura. Predictions are done using a ligand-based approach, based on the similarity between a query molecule and the known ligands of a large collection of protein targets. The result of this study highlighted crucial recommendations for the use of some of the antidiabetic agent groups in diabetic patients. Our findings provide real world evidence supporting the potential clinical benefits of diabetes drug agents in mitigating side effects and development in patients with T2DM.

Background: Anxiety has been increasingly recognized as a relevant contributor to cardiometabolic dysfunction through neuroendocrine, inflammatory, and behavioral mechanisms. However, evidence evaluating the relationship between anxiety symptoms, lifestyle habits, and cardiometabolic risk in large occupational populations remains limited. This study aimed to analyze the association between Goldberg Anxiety and Depression Scale (GADS) scores, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic risk factors in a large cohort of Spanish workers. Methods: A cross-sectional observational study was conducted in 119,336 Spanish workers undergoing routine occupational health examinations between 2021 and 2023. Anxiety symptoms were assessed using the GADS. Lifestyle variables included smoking status, physical activity assessed with the International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ), and adherence to the Mediterranean diet evaluated through the Prevention with Mediterranean Diet (PREDIMED) questionnaire. Anthropometric measurements, blood pressure, lipid profile, fasting glucose, obesity, abdominal obesity, and metabolic syndrome were analyzed. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (ORs) for cardiometabolic abnormalities according to anxiety status and lifestyle factors. Results: Elevated GADS scores were significantly associated with worse cardiometabolic profiles in both sexes, including higher blood pressure, triglycerides, fasting glucose, body mass index, waist circumference, and lower high-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentrations. Workers with elevated anxiety presented markedly higher prevalences of hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, impaired fasting glucose, abdominal obesity, and metabolic syndrome (all p < 0.001). After multivariable adjustment, elevated anxiety remained independently associated with hypertension (OR 6.48; 95% confidence interval (CI) 5.89– 7.09), hypertriglyceridemia (OR 5.31; 95% CI 4.60–6.02), and impaired fasting glucose (OR 5.23; 95% CI 4.64–5.83). Physical inactivity and low adherence to the Mediterranean diet were associated with a less favorable cardiometabolic profile among participants with elevated anxiety scores. Elevated GADS scores were independently associated with all major cardiometabolic outcomes after multivariable adjustment, with the strongest associations observed for hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, and impaired fasting glucose. Conclusions: Elevated GADS scores are strongly associated with adverse cardiometabolic profiles in Spanish workers, particularly when combined with unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. These findings support the integration of mental health assessment and lifestyle interventions into occupational cardiometabolic prevention strategies.

Abstract: Climate change, population growth, and increasing pressure on natural resources pose major challenges to global agricultural production. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising technology for addressing these challenges through precision farming, machine learning, robotic automation, and data-driven decision-making. This study examines the applications of AI in crop management, real-time monitoring, yield prediction, resource optimization, and sustainable agricultural production. The integration of AI with advanced genetic technologies can improve productivity, resource-use efficiency, and climate resilience. However, challenges related to technology, infrastructure, farmer awareness, data availability, affordability, and regulatory frameworks limit its widespread adoption. The study highlights the need for supportive policies, capacity building, digital infrastructure, and collaboration among farmers, researchers, industries, and policymakers. Overall, AI has significant potential to transform modern agriculture, enhance food security, and promote sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural development.

AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up

ABSTRACT Accurate and scalable evaluation of gene‐editing efficiency is crucial for the development of novel editing tools. However, conventional methods are laborious, costly, and low‐throughput. Here, we developed an artificial intelligence (AI)‐driven fluorescent reporter (AR) platform, an integrated system that automates and streamlines the entire evaluation workflow. The AR platform combines an enhanced fluorescent reporter with an AI‐driven analytical pipeline. The dual‐fluorescence reporter system, in which mCherry carrying a PEST domain is paired with GFP, supports Cas variants with diverse PAM requirements and quantifies editing efficiency as the proportion of GFP‐only cells. The platform's AI module, EasyReporter, integrates a deep learning model for automated cell segmentation and quantification with a large language model (LLM)‐based agent for intelligent data interpretation and comprehensive report generation. Editing efficiencies measured by AR correlated with those measured by flow cytometry (Spearman ρ = 0.77) and amplicon sequencing (Spearman ρ = 0.83). The AR platform provides a high‐throughput and automated workflow that accelerates gene‐editing research. In the future, it will be particularly effective for quantifying the efficiency of large‐fragment gene editing, offering a new framework for AI‐empowered biological laboratories.

High-fidelity user simulators are essential for evaluating and training agents in interactive environments. However, current LLM-based simulators struggle with reliability issues, such as goal omission and policy non-compliance. We propose ARGUS (Agenda-dRiven Goal-oriented User Simulator), a neuro-symbolic framework that maintains the user's goal state using a dynamic agenda stack manipulated via symbolic operations. By rigorously decoupling state tracking from natural language generation, ARGUS facilitates strict goal progression and constraint-aligned interactions. For cost-efficient deployment, we distill ARGUS into compact models using a unified pipeline: evaluator-guided SFT followed by online RL with dense step-level rewards. To rigorously evaluate behavioral fidelity, we introduce a rubric-based metric Composite Behavioral Score (CBS). Evaluations on $τ^3$-Bench and MultiWOZ demonstrate the significant superiority of the ARGUS architecture and the efficacy of our training pipeline. Code and data will be released soon.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Scientific papers keep much of their quantitative content in tables and supplementary files, where a number means something only through its header, caption, unit, analytical method, and the conventions of its field. Recovering the rows and columns of a table is therefore not the same as recovering the scientific fact it reports. Most semantic table-interpretation methods assume that a clean table is already available and subsequently map its cells or columns to ontology terms, whereas most publication-level extraction systems are designed for a single domain. We study a middle path: a shared process that reads a paper and its supplementary files, gathers evidence from several parsers and a language model, and reconciles that evidence, while a bounded human-authored task module for each task supplies the domain meaning. The module lists the canonical names the graph may use, the surface forms that map to them, a small set of derivation rules and validity constraints, an identity key, and the bindings used to write RDF. It defines what a task is allowed to emit; it does not try to list every convention of a field. We build four such modules (for drug-discovery chemistry, materials science, machine learning, and mineral geochemistry) in the ArticleMiner framework, and evaluate them on 163 papers, including a new geochemistry benchmark with expert-curated ground truth. In comparisons against a same-LLM few-shot baseline, the point estimates favor ArticleMiner on all four tasks, with uncertainty on the two smaller benchmarks. The geochemistry comparison also includes access to supplementary files, so its improvement cannot be attributed to domain guidance alone.

Abstract Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short‐term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task‐specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum‐of‐care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)‐based skeletal assessment and AI‐augmented dual‐energy X‐ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI‐assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype‐specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient‐reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound‐related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high‐risk surveillance gap during the 90‐day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision‐curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post‐deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. Level of Evidence Level IV.

documents.abstract: Recent dynamic advances in AI technologies have brought about profound transformations in the marketing paradigm and in consumer behavior and interactions. At the heart of this transformation, the relationship between AI agents and consumer behavior stands out as a timely area calling for in-depth investigation in the literature. This study constitutes a bibliometric analysis undertaken to reveal the intellectual accumulation of knowledge in this conceptual domain and to examine the evolution of the literature systematically. To this end, 438 articles indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 2020 and 2026 were subjected to a comprehensive examination. The research first conducted a performance analysis to resolve the quantitative structure of the field, mapping annual publication distributions, the most prolific authors, the most highly cited studies, leading countries, and institutional collaborations. It then carried out citation, co-citation, and co-occurence analyses using science mapping techniques in order to structure the intellectual framework of the field. The findings show that the AI agent literature emerging in the context of consumer behavior is following a growth trend that is gaining momentum in both quantitative and qualitative terms. Thematically, the literature was found to concentrate on the transparency and interpretability of AI algorithms, the implications of these algorithms for consumer attitudes and behavior, the strengthening of human-AI interaction through anthropomorphic design elements, the dark side encompassing ethics, privacy, and trust, and sectoral reflections in the service industry.

documents.abstract: The tourism industry is a social phenomenon that is reliant on various human factors, such as people’s willingness to extend hospitality to others. The hospitality industry is the largest sector within the wider tourism industry, and the term “tourism and hospitality industry” applies widely. The term “hospitality” is used to describe the interaction between a host and a guest, and it originates from Latin. The words hospes and hospitari refer to guests, and hospitalitas denotes entertainment or hospitableness. The chapter will examine how automation is becoming more prevalent in the hospitality industry, focusing on how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies are changing service delivery, customer experiences, and employee roles. It will consider AI applications and their impact on operational efficiency, and customer perceptions of automated interactions. A balance between technological efficiency and human interaction in service encounters is proposed. It will also address the balance between technological efficiency and maintaining the human touch in service encounters.

Abstract Weed infestation is a persistent constraint on the cultivation of medicinal and aromatic crops, reducing yield, quality consistency, raw-material safety, and production standardization. Although herbicide-based weed management has improved labor efficiency, increasing concerns over pesticide residues, herbicide resistance, crop selectivity, and ecological impacts limit its suitability for high-quality herbal medicine production. This review synthesizes the evolution of weed control in medicinal crop systems from manual and mechanical practices to chemical control, integrated weed management, and emerging intelligent–ecological strategies. We propose the concept of Weed Control 4.0 as a crop-specific framework that combines artificial intelligence, intelligent machinery, bioherbicides, and ecological regulation. The review summarizes how microbial and plant-derived bioherbicides suppress weeds through growth inhibition, allelopathic interference, pathogen-mediated damage, and disruption of weed physiological metabolism. It further discusses how machine vision, sensor fusion, robotic platforms, precision spraying, and data-driven decision support can enable real-time weed identification and site-specific intervention. Ecological approaches, including crop rotation, intercropping, mulching, cover crops, allelopathic crops, beneficial insects, and soil microbial manipulation, are evaluated for their potential to suppress weed communities while maintaining soil health and agroecosystem stability. Finally, we identify key challenges for implementation, including medicinal crop-specific weed databases, biosafety and efficacy evaluation of bioherbicides, integration of field machinery with agronomic practices, and residue-safe regulatory standards. Weed Control 4.0 offers a pathway toward sustainable, precise, and residue-safe weed management for the standardized production of high-quality herbal medicines.

This text starts from an AI error incident of September 2026 within US Special Operations Command that ‘almost started a war’. It examines the growing significance of ‘Human Factors’ in European defence as artificial intelligence reshapes relations between humans, military institutions and technological systems. Drawing on European Defence Agency programmes and recent work on trustworthy AI, I suggest that AI changes where and how humans enter military systems, embedding them in increasingly complex sociotechnical relations. Human capacities themselves start to acquire an infrastructural quality, as military systems depend increasingly on how these capacities are organized and managed.

Empirical evidence on how artificial intelligence (AI) relates to student engagement in culturally diverse higher-education settings remains limited. In Chinese university classrooms, where interaction is often teacher-led and asking questions in class can carry a social cost, AI-driven dialogic tools may offer low-pressure opportunities for active participation. This study examined the association between an AI conversational agent (EduBot) and the behavioural, cognitive, emotional and agentic dimensions of engagement among Chinese undergraduates. A mixed-methods quasi-experimental design involved 555 students in four comprehensive (multi-disciplinary, research-intensive) universities, each contributing one introductory course taught in two parallel sections. Within a 15-week semester, intervention sections (n = 278) used EduBot, a Socratic-dialogue agent embedded in the learning management system, for 12 weeks; control sections (n = 277) used teaching-assistant-moderated forums. We measured engagement at three time points with a 21-item four-dimensional engagement scale adapted from an established measure and supplemented it with system logs, 30 student interviews and instructor focus groups. Linear mixed-effects models accounting for the nesting of students within course sections, together with mixed-design ANOVAs, showed Group × Time interactions for behavioural (η 2 p = 0.043, post-test d = 0.71), cognitive (η 2 p = 0.032, d = 0.55), agentic (η 2 p = 0.054, d = 0.57) and emotional engagement (η 2 p = 0.012, d = 0.34), all p ≤ 0.001 after Holm adjustment. Within the intervention group, the number of EduBot sessions predicted post-test engagement after adjustment for baseline scores and covariates. Exploratory moderation analyses indicated larger agentic gains among first-year students and larger cognitive gains among students with lower prior GPA. Thematic analysis identified three hypothesised mechanisms, namely a judgment-free interaction space, scaffolded persistence and temporal flexibility. A Socratic-scaffolded AI agent was associated with higher engagement, most clearly for agentic engagement, which participants described as constrained by classroom norms. The findings support culturally attentive AI design and suggest, tentatively, an equity-enhancing potential. Because the design compared an integrated AI package with usual practice across eight sections, the effects cannot be attributed to single design components.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background: Stem cell bioprocessing requires timely assessment of cell state and control over variable expansion and differentiation. Automated culture can execute predefined steps, whereas adaptive manufacturing uses observations to guide decisions during an ongoing batch.Objective: This review examines how artificial intelligence and machine learning connect process monitoring to prediction and feedback control, and assesses which links have been demonstrated in stem cell systems.Key Content: This topic covers image-based phenotyping, physical and multimodal sensing, growth and differentiation forecasts, process optimization, hybrid models, and proposed digital twins. A descriptive Level 0–6 continuum distinguishes endpoint assessment, monitoring, state estimation, prediction, operator decision support, within-run feedback, and coordinated workflow autonomy. Reported studies demonstrate image-guided adjustments to differentiation, robotic optimization across experiments, and rule-based feedback within a culture. However, these capabilities do not demonstrate autonomous production of a clinically releasable cell product. Translation is further limited by reduced model performance when entire experiments are withheld from training, fragmented datasets, variation across donors and processes, uncertain links between surrogate measures and potency, and the need for model governance.Conclusion: Supervised adaptation and supervised autonomy are credible near-term targets, characterized by bounded, traceable interventions with human oversight and a defined response to uncertainty. Prospective studies should compare adaptive and fixed processes across independent batches and assess cell identity, relevant function, safety-related attributes, and resource use. Claims of full autonomy require verified performance across the manufacturing workflow.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a change agent in healthcare and promises to change clinical decision-making opportunities.AI can be used in nursing to increase efficiency, minimize human error, and support evidence-based practice, among other things.Nevertheless, the attitudes, awareness, and desire of nurses to implement AI are still crucial prerequisites to effective integration into clinical processes.Purpose: This research targeted the awareness, perceived advantages, difficulties, and attitudes of nurses to AI as a decision-making tool and determined the reliability and validity of the tool applied.To add to that, the research has also investigated the effects of demographic characteristics like gender, education, and workplace on perceptions and readiness to embrace AI.Methods: A cross-sectional survey design was used, where 237 nurses in 9 hospitals, clinics, community care, and academic institutions were surveyed to gather data.The Likert scale questions (Q620) included in the structured type of questionnaire were demographic data.We used statistical analysis, which is the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, Cronbach's Alpha reliability, KMO, and Bartlett test of validity, independent sampling t-test, one-way ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis test, Chi-square test, Pearson correlation, and regression analysis.Findings: The data were normally distributed (p > 0.05), and the reliability (Cronbach's Alpha = 0.92) was excellent, as well as the validity (KMO = 0.82; Bartlett's p = 0.001).Cross-group comparisons demonstrated that there was a high level of difference by gender, education, and workplace, and the chi-square analysis indicated that education and AI training were strongly correlated.Pearson correlation also revealed positive relationships between all items in the questionnaire, which showed that there was coherence between awareness, perceived benefits, and adoption.Regression analysis found awareness and understanding to have a strong positive influence on willingness to adopt AI, with age playing a positive but insignificant role.Conclusion: The research concludes that the willingness of nurses to embrace AI is majorly dependent on their awareness and knowledge of the technology, with the educational and workplace context

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the nature, methods, and applications of geographical research. The integration of AI with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Remote Sensing, Global Positioning Systems (GPS), and geospatial big data has created new opportunities for analyzing complex spatial and temporal processes. This study examines the evolving relationship between Artificial Intelligence and Geography, with particular emphasis on its applications, transformative potential, limitations, and future possibilities. The study adopts a descriptive, analytical, and exploratory approach based primarily on secondary data obtained from research articles, academic publications, institutional reports, and relevant scholarly literature. It examines the application of AI across major geographical domains, including Physical Geography, Human Geography, Urban Geography, and Economic Geography. The findings indicate that AI enhances geographical research through automated spatial analysis, image classification, predictive modelling, environmental monitoring, disaster prediction, urban planning, and data-driven decision-making. However, challenges related to data quality, algorithmic bias, transparency, privacy, technological dependence, and unequal access to digital infrastructure remain significant. The study argues that AI should not be viewed as a replacement for geographical expertise but as a complementary technological capability. The future of Geography is therefore likely to be shaped by human–AI collaboration, integrating computational intelligence with geographical reasoning, field knowledge, contextual understanding, and ethical judgement to address emerging spatial and environmental challenges

Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally transforming investment strategies by enabling data-driven decision-making, behavioural insights, and adaptive portfolio management. This chapter examines the evolving role of AI in financial markets by integrating theoretical perspectives, including market efficiency and behavioural finance, with emerging empirical evidence. It explores the growing importance of big data, algorithmic trading, and AI-driven sentiment analysis in shaping market dynamics. The study further analyzes adaptive portfolio strategies, highlighting the role of machine learning and robo-advisory platforms in enhancing efficiency and personalization. In addition, it addresses key regulatory, ethical, and governance challenges, including algorithmic transparency, data privacy, and systemic risk. Through case-based insights, the chapter identifies both opportunities and limitations of AI adoption. It concludes by emphasizing the need for responsible innovation, human AI collaboration, and robust policy frameworks to ensure sustainable and inclusive financial markets.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are transforming the productive core of the global economy, yet public debate remains dominated by single-number claims about the proportion of jobs “at risk”—claims that collapse heterogeneous technologies, tasks, and adoption conditions into a single misleading index. This thesis develops, verifies, and applies a multidimensional framework for assessing the employment consequences of AI and automation across economic sectors. The framework distinguishes four constructs that previous research has often conflated: (D1) digital AI exposure, defined as the proportion of a sector’s task content that current AI systems can technically support or perform; (D2) physical automation, defined as the automatable share of embodied, manual tasks; (D3) adoption, defined as the actual, observed deployment of AI and automation technologies within a sector; and (D4) net employment impact, defined as the estimated medium-term effect on total employment after accounting for displacement, reinstatement, and the creation of new tasks. The thesis proceeds in four stages. First, it reconstructs the technical foundations of machine learning, generative models, and robotics with sufficient rigor for economic analysis, while tracing the economic theory of technology-induced labor reallocation from Ricardo’s machinery question to the contemporary task-based literature. Second, it formalizes the four-dimensional framework through explicit index definitions, aggregation functions, and uncertainty treatment, deriving each dimension from documented methodologies, including task-exposure assessments, adoption surveys, and causal labor-market studies. Third, it applies the framework to nine sectors: information technology, finance and insurance, healthcare, education, manufacturing, construction, transportation and logistics, hospitality and food services, and retail and e-commerce. This analysis synthesizes approximately 280 verified sources, including causal evidence on industrial robots, randomized evaluations of generative AI assistants, and institutional data on technology adoption. Fourth, it examines the implications of the findings, demonstrating that sector-level net employment effects are mediated more strongly by adoption frictions, complementarities, and institutional conditions than by raw technical exposure alone. Employment effects are distributed unevenly across sectors and occupations rather than being confined to aggregate outcomes, and policy interventions can influence outcomes along all four dimensions. Methodologically, the thesis is grounded in a systematic review protocol with preregistered inclusion criteria, a two-pass, point-by-point verification of every citation, reference, and internal cross-reference, and an automated consistency audit whose results are reported in full. Its central conclusion is that a one-size-fits-all approach is inadequate: accurately assessing the labor-market consequences of AI requires keeping the four dimensions analytically distinct, because technologies with identical exposure profiles can produce opposing employment outcomes under different adoption conditions and institutional arrangements. The thesis concludes with scenario analyses for 2035 and a policy agenda addressing education, social protection, taxation, competition, and AI governance.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the food industry by enabling data driven approaches to food quality assessment, safety management, product development, processing, packaging, storage, and supply chain operations. The growing availability of data from sensors, imaging systems, analytical instruments, and digital production platforms has created new opportunities for machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and predictive analytics across the food chain. This chapter reviews the current applications of these technologies in food systems, with particular emphasis on quality and safety assessment, formulation and product development, process optimization, intelligent packaging, shelf life prediction, logistics, and supply chain management. The potential contribution of AI to sustainable food systems is also discussed, including food loss and waste reduction, resource optimization, and circular food production. In addition, emerging applications of generative AI are examined in areas such as food innovation, sensory and consumer research, and research support. Despite these opportunities, challenges related to data quality, model validation, interpretability, privacy, infrastructure, and human oversight remain important considerations. Overall, AI has considerable potential to support more efficient, responsive, and sustainable food systems when computational approaches are integrated with food science expertise and appropriate experimental validation.

With the growing use of digital images in online communication and social media, verifying whether an image is authentic has become increasingly important. Image manipulation techniques such as copy-move, splicing, inpainting, and object removal can change the meaning of visual information. At the same time, JPEG compression and repeated recompression can weaken the forensic traces that are useful for detection. This review looks at two AI-based approaches for detecting digital image forgery. The first study combines Error Level Analysis (ELA) with the VGG-16 convolutional neural network to classify images as original or tampered. The second study focuses on compressed images shared through social networks and uses a modified ShuffleNet V2 architecture for lightweight forgery classification. The two studies are reviewed based on their objectives, datasets, preprocessing or feature representation, deep learning architecture, compression conditions, findings, and limitations. The comparison shows that ELA with VGG-16 can help expose compression-related manipulation artifacts, while the modified ShuffleNet V2 approach focuses on the practical challenge of detecting forgery after JPEG and social-network recompression. The review highlights dataset diversity, compression robustness, computational efficiency, and generalization across different manipulation and sharing conditions as important research gaps. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Digital Image Forgery, Deep Learning, Error Level Analysis, VGG-16,ShuffleNet V2, Image Compression.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly part of higher education's institutional infrastructure, extending beyond teaching and learning to governance, administration, and student support. This study examines how AI Governance Readiness (AIGR) influences Administrative Efficiency through AI (AEAI), AI Fluency Orientation (AIFO), and Student Retention Intentions (SRI), while assessing the mediating roles of AEAI and AIFO and the moderating role of Equity Perception (EPS) in Kazakhstan's higher education sector. Drawing on Dynamic Capability Theory and Sociotechnical Systems Theory, the study develops and empirically tests an institutional capability model using 935 valid responses from students, faculty, academic administrators, and digital administration staff across public and private universities. The scholars analyzed the data using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4.0, supported by RStudio. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity, while the structural model showed adequate explanatory and predictive performance. We assessed common method bias through procedural safeguards and full-collinearity diagnostics, and identified no substantive concerns. The findings show that AIGR is positively associated with AEAI and AIFO, while both constructs positively influence SRI. AEAI and AIFO also significantly mediate the relationship between AIGR and SRI. However, EPS does not significantly moderate the relationships between AI-enabled institutional capabilities and retention intentions. The findings position AI governance as a strategic institutional capability through which universities can improve administrative responsiveness, develop AI-related competencies, and support student continuity. The study contributes empirical evidence from Kazakhstan to the growing literature on responsible AI governance and digital transformation in higher education.

Abstract With an increasing number of devices being installed in agriculture, factories, hospitals, and cities, the need for intelligent, trustworthy, and energy-efficient communication systems is rising. This is one such system: Narrow Band Internet of Things, or NB-IoT, which connects devices at a long range with low-power consumption. But it also has a poor reaction time and is not adaptable to changing situations. This review discusses how artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML), deep learning, and other intelligent methods, are making NB-IoT more adaptable and predictive. By deploying lightweight AI models and edge computing—that is, processing locally on a device—systems are able to better manage wireless signals, save battery life, and improve overall performance. It also discusses several related real-world applications in the area of agriculture, healthcare, industry, and smart cities and achieves benefits such as saving water, early disease diagnosis, predictive machine maintenance, and environmental monitoring. The integration of AI with NB-IoT fosters digital solutions toward sustainability, security, and being human-centric. All the progress made thus far will be of immense utility to decision-makers, engineers, planners of smart cities, and service providers who look to smarter, more affordable, privacy-friendly technology for the future.

Integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare and medical education implies significant opportunities along with significant ethical challenges. Despite the substantial medical student uptake of artificial intelligence globally, little comprehensive assessments of ethical awareness are being conducted. This study aimed to assess artificial intelligence awareness and academic integrity level among University of Khartoum medical students and to examine relationships between the awareness level, demographic factors, artificial intelligence exposure, and tool use behavior. An institutional cross-sectional descriptive study of Years 3–6 medical students at University of Khartoum Faculty of Medicine in 2025 was conducted. A convenience sampling with quota allocation was used, and 349 students responded. The instrument included demographic variables, artificial intelligence exposure measures, and the 32-item Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity Scale. Nonparametric tests were applied. Participants were predominantly female (69.3%) with a mean age of 22.85 years. The median total Artificial Intelligence Ethical Awareness and Academic Integrity score was 4.16, indicative of moderate ethical awareness based on sample-derived empirical tertiles. Privacy and Data Protection were highest (median 4.67), with lowest scores in Transparency and Fairness/Non-Discrimination (3.80). Female students were more aware ( P = .01). No year-based differences observed. While 63.9% had minimal formal artificial intelligence exposure, 51.6% had moderate to high informal exposure. ChatGPT usage was prevalent (94.6%), and Google Gemini/Notebook LM usage was strongly associated with higher awareness ( P = .003). Informal exposure was positively correlated with awareness ( P = .01), but formal exposure was not. Multiple regression indicated that gender, informal exposure, and tool accounted for 11.2% of the variance in awareness. University of Khartoum medical students showed moderate-to-high aggregate artificial intelligence, ethical sensitivity, with areas of privacy protection and accountability being of particular strength. Gaps exist for awareness of transparency and fairness. The dominance of informal learning pathways over formal instruction, and gender variability favoring female students are significant findings. Findings highlight the need for institutional policies and conducting longitudinal research to track the evolution of AI ethics throughout medical training.

documents.abstract: Abstract Climate change and environmental degradation have emerged as two of the most pressing global challenges of the twenty-first century, threatening ecosystems, biodiversity, human health, and sustainable development. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed environmental research and management by enabling advanced data analytics, real-time monitoring, predictive modeling, and intelligent decision-support systems. This review critically examines the applications of AI in addressing environmental and climate-related challenges, including climate forecasting, air and water quality monitoring, biodiversity conservation, precision agriculture, renewable energy optimization, carbon emission assessment, waste management, and disaster risk reduction. Furthermore, The review also identifies current research gaps and highlights future opportunities for developing transparent, energy-efficient, and explainable AI systems that support evidence-based environmental decisionmaking. It concludes that AI has become a transformative tool for accelerating progress toward climate change mitigation, environmental sustainability, and the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration, responsible AI governance, and policy support will be essential to maximize the environmental benefits of AI while minimizing its ecological footprint. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Climate Change; Environmental Sustainability; Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Remote Sensing; Internet of Things; Renewable Energy; Biodiversity Conservation; Sustainable Development Goals.

Introduction Medication errors and adverse drug events remain causes of patient harm, underscoring the need for technologies supporting medication identification, verification, and medication safety. Artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision, optical character recognition (OCR), and digital health technologies are applied to medication recognition. Objective To systematically review AI-based medication recognition systems and characterize recognition tasks, computational approaches, datasets, evaluation, validation, generalizability, deployment, applications, and emerging directions. Methods A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and PubMed/MEDLINE were searched for publications from 1 January 2016 to 4 September 2026, using two conceptual blocks covering medication recognition and AI methods. Of 895 retrieved records, 136 duplicates were removed, and 759 records underwent screening. After full-text assessment, 14 reports were excluded, and 91 studies were included. Title-and-abstract screening yielded 84.72% observed agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.527 ). For methodological assessment, both reviewers independently applied D1–D8 to the 91 included studies before consensus resolution. Across 728 domain-level assessments, observed agreement was 97.66%, with an aggregate Cohen’s κ of 0.959; domain-specific κ values ranged from 0.857 to 1.000. Evidence was synthesized through cross-study analysis and four evidence maps. Results Evidence shows use of detection, classification, OCR/imprint recognition, hybrid and multimodal architectures, alongside few-shot, low-shot, zero-shot, and incremental learning. Applications extend to assistive, mobile, and IoT-enabled systems, medication verification, and clinical decision support. Heterogeneity in datasets, imaging conditions, evaluation protocols, and validation strategies limits comparison and generalizability. External validation, cross-dataset testing, unseen-medication evaluation, prospective deployment, and clinical testing remain limited. Conclusion AI-based medication recognition is evolving from a computer vision task into a digital informatics component supporting medication safety, accessibility, verification, and patient care. Future research should prioritize diverse datasets, leakage control, independent multicenter validation, unseen-medication evaluation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, interoperability, and resource-efficient deployment. Evaluation should extend beyond accuracy to clinical utility, safety, usability, trust, and patient-centered outcomes.

documents.abstract: Urbanization, climate change, increasing energy demand, and rapid infrastructure development have created significant challenges for achieving sustainable and resilient cities. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology that enables data-driven decision-making, intelligent automation, and efficient resource management, making it an important enabler of net-zero and climate-resilient urban systems. This narrative review examines AI applications relevant to urban climate mitigation and adaptation, drawing on literature identified through Google Scholar and ScienceDirect. The review examines the role of machine learning, deep learning, Internet of Things (IoT), big data analytics, cloud computing, digital twins, and generative AI in improving urban energy systems, sustainable transportation, environmental monitoring, infrastructure management, and smart governance. The study also discusses how these technologies contribute to carbon emission reduction, renewable energy integration, climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, and efficient urban planning. In addition, major challenges associated with AI implementation are critically analyzed, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, lack of interoperability, high energy consumption of AI systems, digital inequality, and governance issues. Emerging research trends such as explainable AI, green AI, AI-enabled digital twins, federated learning, and human-centered smart governance are highlighted as important directions for future research. Based on the reviewed literature, the study proposes future research priorities that emphasize interdisciplinary collaboration, responsible AI governance, standardized urban data frameworks, and sustainable policy development. Overall, AI has the potential to accelerate the transition toward intelligent, low-carbon, and climate-resilient cities. The synthesis is qualitative and non-exhaustive, with limitations arising from unavailable original search and screening records and differences between study settings and outcome measures. However, the successful implementation of AI will depend on integrating technological innovation with ethical governance, public participation, and long-term sustainability planning to achieve the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed academic writing, creating new opportunities for students, researchers, and university teachers. AI-powered applications can assist users in generating ideas, organizing arguments, improving grammar, expanding vocabulary, paraphrasing sentences, and editing academic texts. However, the integration of these technologies into higher education also raises important questions concerning academic integrity, authorship, originality, critical thinking, and the reliability of automatically generated information. This article examines the role of AI in academic writing, focusing on its educational benefits, methodological limitations, and ethical implications. The study employs a qualitative, descriptive-analytical approach based on a review of relevant academic literature and international guidelines on generative AI in education and research. The analysis suggests that AI can support the development of academic writing when it is used as an assistive instrument rather than a substitute for independent intellectual work. Particular attention is paid to the responsibilities of students, researchers, and educational institutions in ensuring transparent and responsible AI use. The article argues that effective integration requires AI literacy, critical evaluation of generated content, appropriate disclosure practices, and assessment methods that recognize the importance of human reasoning. It concludes that the educational value of AI depends not simply on technological availability but on the principles governing its application in academic contexts.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT: Background: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in education has expanded rapidly, yet it remains concentrated in higher education and formal schooling in high-income countries. Alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs, which serve out-of-school youth and adults across the Global South, are largely absent from this evidence base. No systematic synthesis has examined how AI is used in these programs, what outcomes it produces, and what conditions shape its adoption. Objective: This protocol describes a mixed-methods systematic review that will identify, appraise, and synthesize empirical evidence on AI use in alternative, nonformal, and adult learning programs in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Methods: The review follows the JBI methodology for mixed-methods systematic reviews and is reported according to PRISMA-P. Searches will cover Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, four regional databases, and grey literature sources for studies published from January 2015 onward. Two reviewers will independently screen records, extract data, and appraise quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Quantitative findings will be synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guideline, with meta-analysis where at least three comparable studies exist. Qualitative findings will be synthesized thematically. Both strands will be integrated through a convergent segregated approach, and certainty of evidence will be rated with GRADE and GRADE-CERQual. Discussion: The review will provide the first consolidated synthesis of AI use in second-chance and adult learning in the Global South. Its findings will inform program managers, teacher developers, and policymakers responsible for programs such as the Philippine Alternative Learning System (ALS). Keywords: artificial intelligence; generative AI; nonformal education; adult learning; Alternative Learning System; Global South; systematic review protocol

documents.abstract: Health insurance fraud imposes substantial financial burdens on healthcare systems and reduces the efficiency of healthcare resource utilization worldwide. Traditional fraud detection approaches often struggle to analyse large and complex healthcare claims data, making artificial intelligence (AI) an increasingly important tool for identifying fraudulent activities. This study systematically reviews global and regional evidence on AI applications in health insurance fraud detection, with particular emphasis on methodological approaches, performance evaluation, and implementation challenges. This systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Seven electronic databases were searched for studies published between 2016 and 2025. Titles and abstracts were screened using the Silvi AI platform, followed by eligibility assessment according to pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were extracted using a standardized framework, and methodological quality was assessed using the Drummond 10-item checklist. From 450 identified records, 33 studies met the eligibility criteria. The included studies demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in datasets, AI methodologies, fraud types, and performance evaluation metrics. Machine learning was the most frequently applied approach, followed by deep learning, graph-based learning, and hybrid AI frameworks. Although AI-based methods consistently improved fraud detection performance, challenges related to dataset imbalance, standardized reporting, interpretability, external validation, and economic evaluation remain significant barriers to widespread implementation. AI demonstrates considerable potential for improving health insurance fraud detection. However, future research should prioritize standardized evaluation frameworks, explainable AI, external validation across diverse healthcare systems, and economic assessment to support the responsible and scalable deployment of AI-enabled fraud detection systems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a vital platform in healthcare and has the potential to completely transform how we care for and maintain our health. This chapter highlights the integration of advanced algorithms into the healthcare ecosystem for the benefit of individuals and society at large, exploring the confluence of AI and healthcare. A new era of individualized and data-driven treatment has arrived through the application of AI in healthcare systems. By analyzing vast amounts of patient data, AI can anticipate illness risks, diagnose conditions, and suggest customized treatment strategies. Advancements in machine learning (ML), neural networks, and natural language processing (NLP) have contributed immensely to this field. This proactive approach to healthcare improves patient outcomes while also reducing stress on the physiological system.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved from science fiction into the clinic with remarkable speed. Machine learning systems now read medical scans, flag sepsis before symptoms declare themselves, draft clinical notes, and coach patients through their smartphones. This article examines the promise and the peril of this transformation in narrative form, and then applies the lens to a single, vivid case: the intertwined epidemics of sleep deprivation and migraine in young adults, where wearable sensors and predictive algorithms are beginning to change how these conditions are detected, studied, and managed. The evidence suggests that AI's greatest near-term contribution is not replacing clinicians but extending their reach — while its greatest dangers, including algorithmic bias, opaque decision making, data privacy erosion, and over-reliance, demand deliberate governance. The article argues that the future of medical AI will be decided less by the sophistication of the algorithms than by the wisdom of the humans who deploy them.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Imaging-guided interventional radiotherapy (IG-IRT) is the standard of care for locally advanced cervical cancer but remains time-consuming and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to improve efficiency and reproducibility. Methods A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between 2010 and 2026 investigating AI-based imaging applications in cervical IRT. Eligible studies included original research evaluating segmentation (targets and organ at risk), planning, reconstruction, image registration and applicator selection. Results Fifty-two studies were included. Deep learning–based segmentation showed variable performance across anatomical structures and studies, with Dice coefficients approaching or exceeding 0.90 for some organs at risk and target volumes in the best-performing models. Individual studies reported shorter processing times, reduced contouring variability, accurate applicator reconstruction, and potential support for applicator selection. However, the substantial methodological and clinical heterogeneity precluded direct comparisons among AI approaches. Conclusions The available studies suggest that AI may support the automation of selected workflow steps and assist treatment-related decision-making in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy. While several applications have achieved high technical performance, most remain at the proof-of-concept stage, and robust external validation and prospective clinical evaluation are needed before routine clinical adoption.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract In recent years, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in immovable cultural heritage research has expanded rapidly, supporting new approaches to heritage documentation, condition assessment, conservation, management, and public communication. In this study, immovable cultural heritage primarily refers to historic buildings, archaeological sites, monuments, cultural landscapes, and other heritage places with fixed spatial locations. Movable cultural objects, museum collections, and intangible cultural heritage are not systematically examined unless the relevant studies directly address the documentation, monitoring, restoration, conservation, or management of immovable heritage. Despite the growing volume of research, existing studies have largely focused on individual technical applications, while comprehensive bibliometric analyses and knowledge-structure mapping from a global perspective remain limited. To address this gap, this study retrieved 382 English-language publications from the Web of Science Core Collection covering the period from 1 January 2015 to 1 October 2025. Using bibliometric methods and analytical tools including VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and ArcGIS, the study examines publication trends, geographical distribution, disciplinary categories, major authors, institutional affiliations, collaboration networks, thematic evolution, and emerging research topics. The results show that publication output increased substantially after 2020. China, Italy, and Spain were among the most productive countries and occupied important positions in the international collaboration network. Major research themes included digital heritage, structural health monitoring, virtual reconstruction, deep learning, remote sensing, and sustainability-related applications. These findings indicate that AI-related research on immovable cultural heritage is strongly represented in engineering, conservation science, computer science, remote sensing, and related technical fields. However, this pattern should not be interpreted as evidence of a general disciplinary shift across cultural heritage studies as a whole. Rather, it reflects the technological orientation of the literature captured by the present search strategy, which was limited to English-language publications indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection. This study maps the development and knowledge structure of AI applications in immovable cultural heritage research and provides quantitative evidence for identifying major research areas, collaboration patterns, methodological tendencies, and future research needs.

Technological innovation has rarely entered human society without resistance.Some of the concerns that accompanied technologies now regarded as indispensable may appear almost incomprehensible today, although they were taken very seriously at the time.The Industrial Revolution provides perhaps the best-known example.In early nineteenth-century England, the Luddites destroyed textile machinery that they perceived as threatening their jobs, skills, and livelihoods.Their reaction was not simply an irrational fear of machines: it also reflected legitimate concerns about profound changes in working conditions and the distribution of the benefits of technological progress.Nevertheless, mechanization continued and eventually transformed manufacturing and society.Other innovations followed similar paths.Railways were initially regarded by some as potentially dangerous to human health.The automobile encountered resistance and restrictive legislation: the British Locomotive Act of 1865 famously required, under certain circumstances, a person carrying a red flag to precede a self-propelled vehicle.Electricity, elevators, vaccination and, much more recently, the Internet all encountered scepticism, resistance or fear before becoming part of everyday life.History does not teach us that every technological innovation is necessarily beneficial.There have been technologies whose harmful consequences became apparent only after widespread adoption.Nor should legitimate concerns about technological change be dismissed as another form of Luddism.History does, however, suggest that genuinely useful technologies tend eventually to become incorporated into ordinary life and professional practice.Artificial intelligence (AI), and particularly generative AI based on large language models (LLMs), appears likely to follow this pattern.The scientific community is now debating whether and how AI should be used in research, scientific writing, peer review and editorial decision-making.Positions range from enthusiasm to considerable concern.Both attitudes are understandable.AI systems can perform tasks that only a few years ago would have seemed extraordinary.At the same time, their limitations-including inaccurate information, fabricated references, bias, lack of transparency and the generation of extremely convincing but incorrect statements-are equally real [1][2][3][4].The question, therefore, should probably no longer be whether scientists will use AI.They already do, and its use will almost certainly increase.A more useful question is: what should we allow AI to do for us, and what must we never delegate to it? Assistance and Delegation Are Not the Same ThingThis distinction, in our view, is fundamental.AI can be an extraordinarily useful scientific assistant.Consider the preparation of a manuscript.AI can identify grammatical and spelling errors, improve the readability of English, suggest more concise formulations, identify repetitions, detect inconsistencies between different sections of a manuscript and help organize complex material.It can assist in searching the literature and in identifying potentially relevant references, provided that these references are subsequently checked against the original sources.

This chapter examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in teacher professional development (PD) within a rapidly evolving global education landscape. It begins by situating AI as a catalyst for shifting from traditional, episodic training models to continuous, data-driven learning ecosystems. Drawing on key theoretical perspectives—including automation to augmentation, socio-technical systems, and diffusion of innovation—the chapter explains how AI supports systemic educational transformation. It further explores intelligent models such as adaptive learning systems, predictive analytics, and AI-enabled coaching that personalize teacher growth. The discussion highlights how AI strengthens instructional leadership and curriculum fidelity through real-time data insights while addressing critical issues of ethics, governance, and digital equity. Finally, it proposes a strategic framework and policy directions to support sustainable, inclusive, and context-responsive AI adoption in education systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in modern education, its potential to improve young people's learning experiences, and its influence on the development of independent thinking. It also discusses challenges associated with AI use, including critical evaluation of information, academic integrity, and digital literacy. Furthermore, the article proposes an original three-step approach designed to encourage students to use artificial intelligence responsibly while developing their analytical and creative thinking skills.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the research landscape and applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in video production through bibliometric mapping and content coding. A Scopus search identified 57 records, of which 24 studies met the eligibility criteria. VOSviewer was used to map thematic and temporal patterns, while content coding examined AI applications, production contexts, stages, purposes, and study types. The findings show that AI is applied across multiple stages of video production, with production efficiency and creative or visual enhancement as recurring purposes. The literature also indicates a shift from task-specific applications toward integrated workflows and greater attention to human–AI collaboration and creative practice.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis
