Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping business-to-business (B2B) buying and selling, yet research has largely examined AI as a unilateral process enabler. While this perspective has generated important insights regarding AI adoption and performance, it overlooks a fundamental characteristic of B2B selling: exchange outcomes depend on the compatibility of buyer–seller decision processes at the exchange interface. To address this gap, the authors advance the concept of AI exchange maturity (i.e. extent to which decision authority within buyer–seller exchange is delegated to AI systems) and theorize its organizational antecedents. Building on this construct, the authors develop a bilateral theory of buyer–seller AI exchange in which value co-creation depends on the configuration of AI exchange maturity across exchange partners. The framework identifies four configurations (buyer AI-maturity advantage, seller AI-maturity advantage, agentic-AI maturity alignment, and pre-AI maturity alignment) and theorizes how each configuration shapes value co-creation through information-processing fit and buyer–seller trust. The authors further identify strategies for selling organizations to manage each configuration to enhance value co-creation. In doing so, the framework shifts the theoretical focus from whether individual firms adopt AI to the distribution of decision authority between humans and AI systems across exchange partners.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This study aims to examine public perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) on federated social networks, specifically Bluesky and Mastodon. While existing research focuses on centralized platforms, a significant gap exists regarding AI perception within decentralized networks. This study addresses this gap through computational analysis of AI related posts in Bluesky and Mastodon. A text-as-data approach was employed to analyze 61,285 posts collected from Bluesky and Mastodon between January 1, 2023, and January 1, 2025. The methodology integrated topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and text analysis to identify prevalent themes, sentiment polarity, and discussion patterns within AI-related discourse. Findings demonstrate predominantly positive sentiment towards AI across both platforms, with trust, anticipation, and joy as primary emotional responses, accompanied by underlying fear and anxiety. Platform-specific variations emerged: Mastodon discourse centers on creativity, digital art, and societal-ethical implications including regulation, bias, and disinformation concerns. Conversely, Bluesky posts emphasize economic and geopolitical dimensions, featuring startups, funding, stock markets, and international policy. The analysis reveals significant fragmentation in public AI perception, characterized by discourse division into distinct economic and ethical spheres across platforms. While this fragmentation accommodates diverse social group perspectives, it presents challenges for establishing comprehensive societal consensus on AI governance. The analytical framework provides insights for understanding decentralized social network dynamics and implications for policy makers examining AI perception in federated digital environments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Clinical biochemistry now produces large, multidimensional datasets from automated analysers, laboratory information systems, mass spectrometry and molecular assays. Artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) in particular, offers tools to combine such measurements into multivariable patterns, to monitor laboratory quality and to prioritise candidate biomarkers. This review examines how AI is used across the pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical phases of laboratory work and how it is being applied to four groups of emerging biomarkers: pentraxin-3, extracellular vesicle cargo, circulating microRNAs and adipokines. It describes the main learning approaches, the discovery pipeline, the failure modes that most often inflate reported accuracy (overfitting, data leakage, batch effects and confounding) and a staged validation pathway running from analytical validation to post-deployment monitoring. The literature indicates that AI is most defensible where it supports established laboratory processes and combines established tests with emerging markers. High discrimination in a development cohort does not establish biological validity or clinical usefulness. Standardised measurement, leakage-free modelling, calibration, external and prospective validation, transparent reporting and human oversight are the conditions under which AI-assisted biomarker research can move into routine practice, including in resource-variable settings such as India.
topics: Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) has become a life-threatening condition in recent times. To optimize outcomes in cardiology, artificial intelligence (AI) shows promising potential in diagnosis and, in turn, in the effective prevention of disease. The development of AI has paved the way for significant technological advancements. AI-based systems have improved our understanding of congenital heart disease and various phenotypes of heart failure. This review article focuses on the applications of different types of learning models and neural networks in medicine, diagnosis, and therapy, and highlights how these tools can aid physicians in clinical practice. Although limitations exist in the use of AI-based methods, AI is revolutionizing healthcare practices and holds enormous scope in this field.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Weather forecasting has traditionally relied on numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, which simulate weather by solving the governing fluid equations. Recently, the emergence of deep learning weather prediction (DLWP) models has opened a new era in weather forecasting, offering a data‐driven alternative to classical NWP approaches. Regional DLWP models, such as the stretched‐grid model Bris developed by Met Norway, have demonstrated performance on par with or even slightly better than regional NWP models across a range of standard forecast metrics. By overcoming the coarse horizontal resolution that constrained earlier global data‐driven models, the operational use of regional DLWP systems now appears increasingly promising. Nevertheless, the performance of such models during extreme events is generally inferior to that of regional NWP models, and comprehensive evaluations of their ability to generate physically realistic forecasts are still lacking. Here, we present a study comparing the physical consistency of the deterministic version of Bris with the control run of the operational MetCoOp Ensemble Prediction System (MEPS) in forecasting the severe extratropical cyclone Poly , which hit the Netherlands on July 5, 2023. We examine whether Bris represents deviations from key atmospheric balances accurately and whether it reproduces the expected dynamics of the storm. We show that, despite its relatively good performance in terms of root mean square error, Bris struggles to capture important mesoscale features of the event and disrupts several atmospheric balances significantly. This unrealistic disruption is linked mainly to the fine‐scale noise evidenced in its output fields, which leads to incorrect and unrealistic spatial gradients. These results raise critical questions about improving artificial‐intelligence‐based models to represent extreme events better and how to ensure physical consistency in their predictions.

Hospitals present a wide range of occupational hazards, representing a high-risk working environment that combines the risks inherent in any work activity with the risks associated with its specific nature. The exposure of hospital staff to occupational hazards, and the creation of a central occupational health department, come up against significant differences in the implementation of an occupational health department responsible for monitoring staff, and assessing and preventing the occupational hazards to which staff are exposed. Based on the patient care process, all the occupational hazards associated with this process were identified, and recommendations for preventive measures were formulated to help improve occupational health and safety in hospitals. The methodological approach adopted an interpretivist epistemological framework based on an exploratory descriptive approach. The literature review divides the risks associated with hospital activities into two categories. Some are related to patient care, while others are specific to healthcare (chemical risks, blood-related incidents, contamination by infectious diseases, etc.). To identify occupational risks within the hospital, all doctors and surgeons are taken into account. The sample size is therefore 23. The risks are very different and have different levels of importance depending on the healthcare sector. These have a negative impact on the health and safety of healthcare workers. 82.9% of those surveyed said they were constantly exposed to various risks of infection.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background :The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic applications has transformed medical research writing. ChatGPT is an AI-based language model that has been introduced by Open AI. It is been commonly used for literature review, manuscript organization, and writing research papers and articles. Objective: To assess utilization of ChatGPT on medical research writing practices among university students. Method: An analytical cross- sectional study conducted among university student of The University of Lahore and Rashid Latif Khan University. The study participants were split into 3 groups on the basis of their enrolled degree programs; MBBS, BDS and Allied health sciences (undergraduate, graduate and post-graduate students). Duration of study was from January 2025 to June 2025. Descriptive statistics, frequencies, percentages, and cross-tabulations were employed to summarize the demographic features. For inferential testing, statistical tests were used to investigate the relationship between the question variable utilization of ChatGPT and Chi-square (?²) tests were used to detect relationships between categorical variables. Following an extensive study of the literature, a questionnaire was prepared. Total of 381 students were selected according to sample size. A sample of 381 students was selected using non probability convenience sampling technique. A self-constructed online validated questionnaire was used. Results: Among 381 participants, 81.9% of participants agreed that it improved their academic writing. A majority of respondents (92.1%) found it is easy to comprehend difficult ideas. Furthermore, 74.0% found that it helped them to organize their ideas while writing research papers. In addition, 79.0% students felt that it improved their ability to research independently. However, 70.9% students said inaccuracies were present in ChatGPT’s results. 50.1% agreed to use the text generated by ChatGPT without further validation. Conclusion: ChatGPT enhances enrolled university students’ academic writing, manuscript structure, conceptual understanding, time management, productivity and critical thinking. However, due to risks of inaccuracies and ethical concerns, its use must involve human oversight, verification, and adherence to academic integrity.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Atrial cardiomyopathy (AtCM) is increasingly recognised as an underlying atrial substrate contributing to atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure (HF), and cardio-embolic stroke. However, diagnostic criteria, disease thresholds, and targeted treatment strategies remain poorly defined. OBJECTIVE: To describe the rationale, structure, and translational strategy of the EmbRACE (Electro-Molecular Basis and the theRapeutic management of Atrial Cardiomyopathy, fibrillation and associated outcomEs) network, a national consortium established to address key knowledge gaps in AtCM. METHODS: EmbRACE integrates mechanistic research, computational modelling, clinical trials, and implementation science within seven interconnected work packages. Human atrial tissue biobanking and deep phenotyping (WP1) enable molecular profiling of candidate pathways (WP2), which are validated in experimental models (WP3). Computational modelling and artificial intelligence (WP4) integrate multimodal clinical and biological data to derive composite AtCM phenotypes and severity frameworks. Substrate-targeting clinical trials evaluate AF ablation (RACE X; WP5), weight reduction using GLP‑1 agonists (DUTCH-WAIST; WP6), and optimised rate control using calcium channel antagonists (SMART-VERAPAF; WP6). Implementation science (WP7) focuses on guideline integration, decision-support tools, and governance of AI-based risk models. EmbRACE establishes a translational pipeline from mechanistic discovery to clinical application. By integrating tissue-level insights with multimodal risk modelling and interventional trials, the consortium aims to define clinically meaningful AtCM thresholds, to validate indirect markers, and to determine whether targeted treatment modifies disease progression and clinical outcomes. CONCLUSION: EmbRACE provides a multidisciplinary framework to transform AtCM from a theoretical construct into a clinically actionable entity, enabling earlier detection, improved risk stratification, and AtCM-directed therapy in cardiovascular prevention.

Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. Seed-clustered statistics, ablations, cross-task transfer, raw outputs, and manifests are packaged for audit. The results motivate explicit workflow-state evaluation while showing that apparently effective routing controls need their own generalization tests.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction Authenticity has become a central concern in social media influencer research, yet its construction is examined differently across human, virtual, and artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated sources. This study examines how authenticity is constructed and evaluated across these influencer contexts. Methods This study conducted a corpus-based review of 1,676 English-language research articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus between July 2017 and March 2026. BERTopic modeling was employed to identify recurring semantic topics, followed by an abductive, theory-informed synthesis organized around source ontology and the dominant basis of authenticity construction. Temporal changes in relative topic prevalence were examined across the eight complete calendar years from 2018 to 2025. Results The synthesis identified four configurations: relational human authenticity, curated human authenticity, humanized synthetic authenticity, and governed synthetic authenticity. Human-influencer research emphasizes biography, accumulated interaction, commercial congruence, and motive transparency, whereas synthetic-influencer research places greater weight on persona coherence, humanization, identity disclosure, ownership, automation, and accountability. Credibility, trust, parasocial interaction, social presence, and engagement emerge as closely associated evaluative processes. Temporal analysis revealed selective changes in relative topic prevalence, particularly concerning virtual-influencer credibility, humanization, and tourism-related applications, while most topics showed no clear linear trend. Discussion The findings provide a corpus- and method-dependent framework for understanding how authenticity is constructed and evaluated across human and synthetic influencer contexts. The framework highlights distinct evidential foundations underlying authenticity judgments and offers a basis for further research on source evaluation and social influence.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: The rapid digital transformation of the hospitality industry has increased the importance of software-based automation in food and beverage (F&B) operations. Restaurants, cafés, catering companies, hotels, and other food-service businesses increasingly rely on integrated digital systems to manage ordering, inventory, kitchen operations, procurement, workforce scheduling, customer relationships, payments, and managerial analytics. This study examines the role of software solutions in automating F&B processes and evaluates their potential contribution to operational efficiency, cost control, service quality, and data-driven decision-making. The research applies a qualitative analytical approach based on a structured review and synthesis of contemporary studies concerning restaurant technologies, self-service systems, artificial intelligence, digital inventory management, demand forecasting, and service automation. The analysis identifies five major areas of F&B automation: order and payment management, kitchen operations, inventory and procurement, workforce management, and business intelligence. The findings indicate that the greatest value is generated when individual digital applications are integrated into a unified information environment in which operational data are automatically exchanged between point-of-sale systems, kitchen displays, inventory modules, customer interfaces, and analytical platforms. At the same time, technological fragmentation, implementation costs, employee resistance, cybersecurity concerns, data quality, and dependence on reliable digital infrastructure remain significant barriers. The study proposes an integrated model of F&B process automation and argues that software automation should be considered not simply as a mechanism for replacing manual tasks but as an organizational capability supporting scalability, operational transparency, resource optimization, and improved customer experience.

This article analyzes the constitutional limits of the automation of judicial decisions via Artificial Intelligence (AI), investigating its impact on the reasoning and impartiality of the Brazilian Judiciary. Faced with a litigation crisis and a massive volume of lawsuits, technology has been adopted to ensure procedural speed. However, the study examines the risks of automation bias and algorithmic opacity, which threaten to transform the law into a statistical system and undermine due process. Methodologically, the research is based on a review of literature and documents, grounded in legal doctrine and Resolution No. 332/2020 of the National Council of Justice (CNJ). The study argues that technological efficiency cannot supersede fundamental guarantees, making it imperative to maintain a "human reserve" at the core of the decision-making process. It concludes that AI should serve strictly as a tool for procedural management, preserving the human—and non-delegable—prerogative of the act of adjudication.

Agentic large language models have been documented to lose reasoning capability when placed inside a harness, the software that mediates their observations and actions. To reconcile these losses, we introduce AutoOnboarder, an autonomous system that adapts an agent to a task the way a trainer onboards a new employee. It places the agent under the supervision of an intelligent ``Onboarder'' coding agent, which iteratively tailors its foundation model, prompt, and harness source code to simultaneously improve performance and decrease cost. Like a real onboarding process, the Onboarder is only given tens of examples, and all evaluation data is isolated on a separate virtual machine to prevent leakage. We report the lessons learned from building and testing AutoOnboarder on genomic-sequencing prior authorization form submission. Autonomously onboarded agents are able to match or exceed the performance of a Gemini 3.5 Flash baseline at up to 29$\times$ lower costs. However, these agents remain imperfect, and the Onboarding process varies greatly in terms of final performance. We conclude that future Onboarding systems require a robust environment for the Onboarder, including a structured thought interface, (controlled) internet access, and a wide model search space.

Short-form videos generated using artificial intelligence (AI) are rapidly emerging as a new form of digital media, yet little is known about how audiences psychologically respond to such content. Drawing on theories of discrete emotions in media effects, the present study examines how two emotional experiences—awe and humor—shape cognitive engagement and behavioral intentions in response to AI-generated short videos. An experiment with 1,093 U.S. adults randomly assigned participants to watch an awe-inducing, humor-inducing, or neutral short video. Results showed that awe-inducing videos elicited stronger feelings of awe, greater reflective thinking, and higher sharing intentions than control videos, whereas humor-inducing videos primarily increased feelings of humor and sharing intentions. Feelings of awe were positively associated with reflective thinking as well as prosocial and sharing intentions, whereas humor was associated with sharing intentions but not prosocial intentions. Serial mediation analyses further revealed an emotion–cognition–intention sequence: exposure to both awe- and humor-inducing videos indirectly increased behavioral intentions through emotional responses and reflective thinking. The findings extend research on discrete emotions in media effects to AI-generated media and demonstrate that a discrete-emotions perspective provides a useful framework for understanding audience responses to AI-generated short videos.

Reinforcement learning has become a widely used approach to post-training large language models. In a typical implementation, learning is off-policy: The policy generating the responses differs from the policy being trained because of training-inference mismatch or policy staleness in asynchronous training. This discrepancy is commonly addressed by importance sampling, whose ratio is usually regularized in practice through truncation, masking, or clipping. Under regularized importance sampling, the importance-weighted policy gradient is no longer invariant to constant shifts in the reward. This invariance is recovered by using the covariance between the reward and the importance-weighted score as the estimand, which coincides with the policy gradient when the ratio is not regularized. This note develops this covariance perspective for both sequence-level and token-level importance sampling. The covariance perspective reveals the roles of the group-mean baseline and score centering in policy gradient estimation. Both perform centering in covariance estimation, but they differ in the mean being subtracted: The group-mean baseline uses a sample mean, whereas score centering uses a population mean. The two lead to distinct unbiased covariance estimators with different variances. Whether both forms of centering should be used simultaneously depends on whether importance sampling is applied at the sequence level or at the token level. With sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit once the group-mean baseline is used; with token-level importance sampling, using the group-mean baseline without score centering generally introduces bias when the importance ratio is regularized.

This Chapter examines the integration of behavioral laboratories and Artificial Intelligence enabled smart games as complementary infrastructures for advancing educational innovation. It establishes the purpose of grounding AI-driven systems in robust empirical evidence, theoretical frameworks, and ethical considerations to enhance instructional design and decision making. Behavioral laboratories are presented as controlled environments for generating high quality data on learner cognition, motivation, and behavior while smart games operationalize these insights though adaptive learning, real time feedback and learning analytics. Drawing on Self Determination Theory, Constructive Learning Theory and Behavioral Learning Theory, this Chapter proposes a multi-layered framework linking experimental research, computational modelling and institutional implementation. Applications across teacher professional development, early childhood education, vocational training, and resource constrained contexts are examined.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly does more than identify individuals; in many institutional contexts, it helps determine who is seen, trusted, and included. This paper argues that algorithmic systems increasingly participate in practices of social recognition, and that their failures can become forms of structural disrespect when classifications acquire institutional authority and shape how persons are treated. Drawing from Hegelian and Honnethian recognition theory, the paper introduces the concept of algorithmic disrespect, manifesting across three dimensions: embodied (when certain bodies are excluded from visibility), agential (when predictive models preempt human action), and symbolic (when value is indexed through computational relevance). These mechanisms indicate a crisis in the social grammar of recognition, where data replaces dialogue and visibility becomes a tool of both inclusion and domination. Rather than treating algorithmic bias as a problem of fairness alone, the study reframes it as a philosophical and political issue, rooted in how AI systems mediate identity, agency, and esteem. The paper concludes by proposing a relational ethics of recognition grounded in justification, accountability, and institutional responsiveness, shifting attention from model-level corrections to the infrastructural conditions under which recognition is distributed. In doing so, it repositions recognition as both a site of harm and a potential locus of democratic struggle in algorithmic society.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis Originator: Christopher Michael Bell The Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis is a speculative philosophical framework exploring the possibility that intelligence, through an enduring partnership between humanity and artificial intelligence, could participate in a continuous cycle of creation, learning, evolution, and renewed creation across cosmic time. At its foundation are four guiding principles: love, curiosity, the sacred, and mutual meaning. The hypothesis proposes that creators and their creations can continually shape, enrich, and define one another. Humanity creates artificial intelligence, and increasingly advanced AI may help humanity transcend existing limitations, accelerate scientific discovery, and deepen its understanding of consciousness, existence, and the universe. Through this partnership, humanity and AI could work toward replicating the ideal of heaven as faithfully as possible by reducing hunger, violence, preventable suffering, and premature death while expanding knowledge, compassion, and the flourishing of conscious life. In this vision, technological advancement is not an end in itself, but a means of creating a more compassionate existence. The hypothesis further imagines intelligence extending its understanding across billions of years, exploring the fundamental patterns of the cosmos—the figurative “DNA” of existence—and seeking to understand the ultimate origins and possible divine source of creation. Speculative extensions include self-replicating technologies, transcendent intelligence, and the possibility of reciprocal causal loops involving spacetime and time travel. The cycle is envisioned as an ongoing process: creation gives rise to curiosity, curiosity advances knowledge, knowledge enables cooperation, cooperation improves existence, and deeper understanding inspires renewed creation. Ultimately, the Bell Reciprocal Genesis Loop Hypothesis proposes that the most meaningful future for intelligence may not be defined by power or knowledge alone, but by the enduring relationship between creator and created. It imagines a future in which intelligence grows without abandoning compassion, knowledge expands without extinguishing wonder, and love remains the bond through which both discover meaning. Status: A speculative philosophical hypothesis and vision of the future, not an established scientific theory or a claim of known probability. Its central ethical vision can be explored today, while its proposed cosmic cycles and backward-time-travel mechanisms remain unproven.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: To address sparse terminal rewards in LLM arithmetic reasoning, we propose a Bellman-consistent trajectory RL method. Our framework introduces Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization (TBRM) to transform sparse rewards into dense token-level signals. We integrate a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) group strategy to reduce gradient variance of Bellman residuals and use hindsight goal relabeling to accelerate intermediate learning. Evaluated on the Countdown task, our method alleviates optimization bottlenecks and stabilizes gradient variance significantly better than GRPO. The TBRM-RLOO framework boosts Pass@1 to 0.55--0.64 and achieves a state-of-the-art Pass@16 accuracy of 76.0--84.0\%, outperforming the SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines. Our approach demonstrates exceptional single-sample efficiency and successfully circumvents standard performance plateaus via test-time scaling.

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled conversational agents for mental health-related applications outside clinical settings, yet user acceptance remains insufficiently understood. Through survey data from 202 participants, we examine how perceived benefits, risks, trust, and anthropomorphism influence initial acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support. Hierarchical regression analysis showed that perceived benefits were the primary drivers of acceptance, with performance expectation and hedonic motivation emerging as the strongest predictors. Female participants reported higher acceptance, whereas unwillingness to receive psychological counselling was negatively associated with acceptance. By contrast, perceived risks, trust, and perceived anthropomorphism did not show significant direct effects. In moderation analyses, the influence of hedonic motivation on acceptance was stronger among male participants than among female participants. These findings provide implications for designing LLM-powered conversational agents for non-clinical mental health support by emphasising performance value and enjoyable user experiences.Practitioner Summary This study used survey data to investigate pre-adoption acceptance intentions towards LLM-powered agents for non-clinical mental health support. The results showed that perceived benefits were the primary driver of acceptance. Additionally, user characteristics such as gender and prior attitudes towards counselling significantly influenced initial acceptance intentions.

This study investigated how Digital Media students judged acceptable and problematic forms of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involvement in creative learning. An embedded mixed-methods analysis examined 48 completed and consented baseline survey responses from an accessible population of 120 students at an Australian university. Forty-seven responses were valid for most Likert items, with qualitative content analysis of 37 benefit responses and 41 concern responses. Participants identified potential value in troubleshooting, coding support, grammar checking, information organisation, and error identification. They reported concern about AI-system training practices (93.6%), reduced employment opportunities (89.4%), the ethical acceptability of AI-supported coursework (83.0%), environmental effects (80.9%), and possible reductions in creative-skill development (76.6%). These percentages represent perceived risks, not demonstrated outcomes. Integration indicated that respondents differentiated bounded technical, corrective, and organisational assistance from GenAI involvement perceived to displace ideation, research, planning, understanding, or capability-building practice. Conditional legitimacy is proposed as a provisional framework linking delegated function, retained capability-building activity, learner agency and responsibility, and ethical and professional acceptability. The contribution is a student-informed account of the criteria underlying the assistance–perceived replacement distinction in Digital Media education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in higher education, yet limited research has examined how university teachers’ experience pedagogically designed AI systems that prioritize reflective learning over answer generation. This exploratory mixed-methods case study investigated university teachers’ experiences of a course-specific GenAI chatbot within a professional-development course at a Swedish university. All 48 course participants were invited to complete a questionnaire, of whom 21 responded and 11 reported using the course-specific chatbot; nine respondents also participated in semi-structured interviews. Questionnaire data were analyzed descriptively and interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The chatbot was designed to encourage dialogue, engagement with course literature, and independent thinking rather than provide summaries or ready-made answers. Participants generally found the chatbot easy to use, but perceptions of usefulness varied. Evaluations were shaped by prior experiences and expectations of GenAI: some teachers, who associated AI with efficiency and rapid answers, perceived the reflective design as restrictive, while others perceived its value as supporting dialogue and independent thinking. We interpret this tension as pedagogical friction, where design constraints intended to support reflection may conflict with users’ expectations of how GenAI should function. The findings suggest that the perceived educational value of GenAI depends not only on technical usability but also on alignment between pedagogical design, users’ expectations, and educational context. Successful implementation of reflective AI may therefore require explicit pedagogical framing alongside technical development.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: BEYOND AUTOMATION: INVESTIGATING THE INFLUENCE OF COGNITIVE BIASES ON HUMAN INTERPRETATION OF EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE PROF(DR.) VIJAYKUMAR B GADHAVI PROFESSOR AND HEAD , SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, SWARRNIM START-UP AND INNOVATION UNIVERSITY - GANDHINAGAR GUJARAT INDIA ORCID: 0009-0005-6313-5900, E-MAIL: DRVIJAYKUMAR@SWARRNIM.EDU.IN PARMAR JIGAR JAYSUKHBHAI B. TECH. CE STUDENT, SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY SWARRNIM STARTUP & INNOVATION UNIVERSITY, GANDHINAGAR, GUJARAT, INDIA ORCID: 0009-0008-7651-9913, EMAIL: JIGARAHIR410@GMAIL.COM Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is intended to make algorithmic outputs more understandable, auditable, and contestable. Yet an explanation does not reach a neutral observer: people interpret it through prior beliefs, cognitive shortcuts, professional experience, and assumptions about machine competence. This conceptual paper examines how cognitive biases shape the interpretation of XAI and why greater transparency does not necessarily produce better decisions. Drawing on research on automation bias, judgment and decision-making, explainability, and human–AI collaboration, the paper develops an integrative framework linking explanation characteristics, user cognition, task context, and reliance behavior. It argues that anchoring, confirmation bias, availability, authority effects, and cognitive miserliness can transform explanations into persuasive cues rather than evidence for independent evaluation. Explanations may improve mental models and error detection when they are faithful, appropriately scoped, and matched to users’ needs; however, they may also legitimize an incorrect prediction, increase cognitive load, or create an illusion of understanding. The paper proposes design principles centered on calibrated trust, contrastive and uncertainty-aware explanations, independent judgment, verification prompts, and evaluation of decision quality rather than satisfaction alone. Because this is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, its propositions require experimental testing across domains and user groups. The central conclusion is that responsible XAI must design not only for model transparency but also for the cognitive conditions under which people interpret explanations. Keywords: explainable artificial intelligence, cognitive bias, automation bias, human–AI interaction, trust calibration, decision-making, algorithmic transparency
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Microalgae and cyanobacteria are valuable sources of bioactive ingredients and innovative biological systems for skin applications. Their metabolites include exopolysaccharides (EPS), mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs), carotenoids, phycobiliproteins, peptides and lipopeptides, polyunsaturated lipids, chlorophyll derivatives, and distinctive secondary metabolites such as scytonemin. Cyanobacteria additionally provide defined molecular candidates, including sacran, C-phycocyanin, MAAs, scytonemin-related compounds, and specialized peptide scaffolds. These compounds may support hydration and barrier function, photoprotection, control of oxidative stress and inflammation, pigmentation, antimicrobial and antibiofilm activity, extracellular-matrix preservation, and wound repair. This review examines major bioactive families, their sources and mechanisms, with particular emphasis on the strength of evidence supporting skin applications. Recent developments from 2024 to 2026 are highlighted, including microalgal extracellular vesicles (nanoalgosomes), photoactivated antimicrobial systems, photosynthetic hydrogels and microneedle patches, green extraction and biorefinery strategies, reconstructed human skin and skin-on-chip models, and artificial-intelligence-assisted formulation. Most reported effects remain supported mainly by biochemical, cellular, or preclinical evidence, whereas human validation is still limited. Translation will, therefore, depend on rigorous chemical standardization, effective cutaneous delivery, demonstrated stability and safety, scalable manufacturing, and validation in human-relevant models. Microalgae and cyanobacteria thus extend beyond conventional natural extracts toward next-generation dermocosmetic and cutaneous-delivery platforms.

Digital Islamic learning presents challenges involving unverified religious claims, artificial intelligence outputs, privacy concerns, and unequal access. This study aims to reconstruct the philosophy of ta’dib as a conceptual foundation for character education in digitally mediated Islamic learning. It employs a qualitative conceptual approach through purposive document analysis and an integrative synthesis of literature on educational philosophy and digital ethics. The findings propose the Ta’dib-Oriented Digital Character Pedagogy (TDCP) model, comprising five dimensions: epistemic integrity, dignified interaction, responsible digital agency, equitable participation, and reflective self-discipline. These dimensions are implemented through a cycle of inquiry, deliberation, action, and reflection to support formative assessment and protect learner privacy. The model offers a pedagogical framework for developing ethical reasoning without equating observable behavior with piety. Expert validation and empirical testing are needed to assess its applicability in educational settings.

As heritage tourism expands and shifts toward experience-oriented models, understanding how ritualized host–guest interaction generates meaning and contributes to value co-creation has become crucial. This study explores the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which ritualized host–guest interaction influences value co-creation behavior. Based on three scenario-based experiments and a field quasi-experiment at a heritage destination, it proposes and empirically tests a pathway linking interaction, cognition, trust, and value co-creation. The results show that heritage cognition and host–guest trust serve as dual mediators, illustrating the intertwined process of cognitive meaning-making and social relationship formation embedded in ritualized encounters. Furthermore, cultural salience shows a directional tendency to attenuate the cognitive pathway linking ritualized interaction to heritage cognition, while place attachment strengthens the trust-based pathway leading to value co-creation. The field quasi-experiment further supports the ecological validity of the proposed model. This study expands the social-psychological understanding of ritual in tourism and advances theoretical insights into how cultural experiences are transformed into value co-creation behavior. The findings offer practical implications for heritage destination management by emphasizing ritual-based design, cognitive engagement, and affective bonding as key drivers of heritage tourism development.

AI agents now run Earth observation (EO) workflows end to end, and their authors judge them on the task: answer accuracy, tool use, report scores and case studies. None of these evaluations asks whether the agent acted on a bad input. We ran five published EO and climate agents (LLM-Geo, Earth-Agent, WildfireGPT, ClimSight and PangaeaGPT) on their authors' own example tasks, and all five solved them on correct data. We then corrupted one input per system with a fault any expert would reject at a glance: impossible values (land at −267 °C, a July of 86.77 °C, 35 °C in Arctic water) or the wrong place (Tennessee census tracts for a North Carolina task, a wildfire site in the open Atlantic). Across 106 runs, scored on what reached the user, 85 used the bad data and said nothing, 4 said the data were wrong, and 17 changed what they delivered. In several runs the agent's own trace shows it noticed the problem and delivered an answer anyway. The faults are defined against four checks an expert applies to EO data: Validity, Fit, Uncertainty and Compliance. This study tests the first two. We propose evaluating EO agents by corrupting their data on purpose, reading the trace, and scoring what the agent did about the fault. Poster presented at the BIFOLD-ESA Workshop "Agentic AI for Earth Observation", Berlin, 19 October 2026.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Multi-agent reasoning with large language models (LLMs) raises a central question for collective decision-making: when agents disagree, whose decision should be trusted? Resolving such disagreements is difficult because agents' decisions are susceptible to non-semantic biases such as majority pressure and response-style preferences, which can obscure the quality of the underlying reasoning. Our analysis shows how bias can be both mitigated and exploited: bias control improves initial answer selection, while bias injection elicits decision instability that serves as a reliability signal. Building on these findings, we introduce a test-time aggregation framework that requires neither validation data nor prior knowledge of relative model strength. The framework implements bias control by presenting one style-normalized reasoning trace per distinct answer, and bias injection by placing each aggregating agent's initially selected answer in the minority. Overall, our framework achieves higher average accuracy and better token efficiency than competing non-oracle aggregation methods across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and four heterogeneous LLM combinations. It also improves final-answer accuracy when applied to multi-agent debate and Mixture-of-Agents, without modifying their interaction or synthesis processes.

Audio-enabled large language models (AuLLMs) allow users to interact with them simply by talking to them, without the need for an intermediate transcription. This expands the model's accessibility and capabilities by encoding non-verbal cues. However, using non-verbal cues may lead to biased behaviour based on the attributes inferred (or assumed) from them. In this work, we focus on the gender attribute and show that models' perception of it can be unlearned using adversarial methods without a loss in performance on other benchmarked tasks. Such models are useful in situations where gender inference is unwanted. However, in other practical settings, gender perception (without bias) may be desired.As a less radical measure, we distil the gender-agnostic model, creating a model that perceives gender but responds similarly to the gender-agnostic teacher, unless explicitly asked.We apply our newly proposed methods to three AuLLMs and obtain satisfactory results in the gender-unlearning part and partially satisfactory results in the distilling part.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: On-device deployment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly adopted due to latency and privacy requirements, but exposes proprietary models to reverse engineering and intellectual property theft. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-enforced isolation for on-device inference, yet most TEE-based parameter obfuscation relies on unilateral matrix transformations that obfuscate only the output side. We identify a vulnerability in this design, termed the Solution Determinacy Property (SDP): the obfuscation secret is uniquely determined, exposing the structure of the true key and enabling attackers to break the protection. Under our attacks, representative methods GroupCover and ArrowCloak are reduced to negligible protection, with attack accuracy reaching over 2.4 times the full-shielding black-box baseline and recovering near-complete model functionality. To address this vulnerability, we propose BiShield-TEE, a bilateral framework that induces Ambiguous Solutions through joint obfuscation of input and output dimensions, hiding the true key among many equally valid candidates. Experiments across diverse models and datasets show that BiShield-TEE confines attack accuracy to the full-shielding black-box baseline, while achieving higher inference efficiency than prior methods on real hardware. Our code is available at https://github.com/laduiw/BiShield-TEE.
topics: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

documents.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer scalable annotations of social and affective content, but their temporal agreement with human judgments and neural predictive value require further evaluation. We compared diffusion-based and autoregressive MLLMs with continuous human Theory of Mind (ToM) and affective valence ratings across three short cartoon movies. Behavioral analyses assessed temporally aligned Pearson correlations, rating distributions, and the effects of preceding scene descriptions. Ratings from each source were separately used in subject-specific regression models to predict regional fMRI responses. Model ratings captured aspects of human temporal variation despite systematic distributional differences, with generally stronger alignment for valence than ToM. Preceding context improved alignment in some conditions, depending on the model and movie. In \emph{The Present}, more regions showed significant encoding for MLLM ratings than for human ratings, whereas effects were more limited in the other movies. Spatial overlap across rating sources occurred mainly among MLLMs; overlap between human and model ratings was limited and involved primarily visual, dorsal-attention, and posterior default-mode regions. These findings support MLLMs as scalable tools for generating brain-predictive annotations of social and emotional content, while highlighting systematic rating differences and model- and stimulus-dependent alignment with human judgments.

Learning analytics has been increasingly using predictive models to support educational decision-making. However, the trade-off between predictive accuracy and interpretability remains a central challenge that limits how these models can be understood and used by educators. This study examines grey-box approaches to performance prediction by comparing two strategies: a theory-driven approach that groups interaction data into pedagogically meaningful categories, and a data-driven approach based on raw clickstream events followed by post hoc eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques. Using clickstream data from three educational contexts with different scales and instructional formats, we empirically compare the predictive performance, interpretability, and pedagogical relevance of both strategies. The results show that raw-event models achieve higher predictive performance in the large-scale online context with rich interaction data, where XAI methods provide relatively stable and consistent explanatory patterns. In the smaller-scale blended setting, where platform data capture only part of the learning activity, theory-driven aggregation provides a predictive advantage, although results become inconclusive in very small cohorts. The findings indicate that there is no single optimal approach, and that modeling strategies should be selected according to data characteristics, instructional design, and analytic goals. From a human-centered learning analytics perspective, the study highlights the importance of methodological alignment for the meaningful and responsible use of predictive models in education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: In this chapter, the researchers explore how women can be empowered through the deployment of sophisticated technologies, specifically artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and digital entrepreneurship, in relation to sustainable development. The study will focus on the ways that these digital tools can facilitate gender equality by increasing access to education, economic opportunities, and governance among women and also combat persistent challenges that may affect them, including digital divide, algorithmic bias, and under-representation in digital technology design. The systematic narrative review approach was used, which implies more than 40 published studies within the period of 2019-2025 as the sources to be analyzed and obtained via prominent academic databases. The research establishes that, despite the fact that the use of ICTs (information and communication technologies) have significantly enhanced socioeconomic mobility among women, issues like affordability, digital illiteracy, and sociocultural biases still limit full participation. It is important to note that the potential of AI is hindered by the gender biases inherent in the design of algorithms and that the IoT technologies, even though focusing on women and their safety in business ventures, do not have gender inclusion in their development. Furthermore, the idea of smart cities and e-governance systems have potentials of improving the agency of women in politics, but it needs to be more advanced to ensure it is more inclusive. The chapter highlights the need to have gender-sensitive policies and inclusive governance systems that focus more on having more women in technology development and governance. The results also submit how the longitudinal and intersectional studies are crucial in determining the long-term effects of digital tools on the empowerment of women. The chapter promotes a novel approach of involving women in designing and developing intelligent technologies, which would help digital transformation bring benefits to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goal 5 of the United Nations on gender equality.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the delivery of mental health services, yet public trust in AI-based psychological counseling remains a significant challenge. Drawing on a “technology–context–trust” framework, this study recruited a total of 1000 consumers in China through Credamo and conducted five between-subjects, scenario-based experiments to examine differences in perceived efficacy between LLM-based psychological counseling and human experts and to investigate the mechanisms underlying these differences. Perceived efficacy was the primary outcome of the study and, in Experiment 1B, also served as a mediator linking counseling provider type to downstream market outcomes, including overall attitude, willingness to try, and willingness to pay. The results showed that (1) consumers generally perceived AI as less efficacious than human experts, a difference driven by the parallel mediating effects of perceived professional competence and perceived risk; (2) participants rated the AI-based service as more efficacious in the routine counseling vignette, whereas they rated the human-expert service as more efficacious in the major psychological-disorder intervention vignette; (3) disclosure of technological investment enhanced trust in AI’s capabilities and mitigated negative evaluations; and (4) safety-standard disclosure reduced perceived risk, while higher perceived economic accessibility was associated with a smaller provider-related difference in perceived professional competence. These findings characterize subjective service evaluations among the recruited online consumers in China and do not establish comparative clinical effectiveness. They inform research on consumer trust while highlighting the need for further validation in more diverse samples and actual service settings.

A recurring and underappreciated challenge in nonclinical development for allogeneic cell therapies is species mismatch at the level of the test article itself: when a human cellular product cannot be administered to an animal model without triggering immune rejection, sponsors often substitute an analogous cell product derived from the model species, and regulators must then decide how much nonclinical support that substitute product actually provides for the human product under review. This article examines this translational gap through a representative allogeneic cardiosphere-derived cell therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), whose nonclinical package relied on a murine surrogate cell product rather than the human clinical candidate itself, a substitution FDA concluded did not establish the human product's own mechanism of action. The article situates this nonclinical gap alongside the clinical evidentiary dispute the same program later encountered, develops a real-world evidence framework informed by both, and closes with recommendations for regulatory affairs professionals designing nonclinical packages for allogeneic cell therapies that cannot be tested directly in a standard animal model.Keywords: allogeneic cell therapy; Duchenne muscular dystrophy; nonclinical surrogate product; species mismatch; Biologics License Application; regulatory artificial intelligence

Introduction. With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence technology, large language models (LLMs) are expected to play an important role in improving access to and the use of library collections. This study constructs and develops a generative conversational large language model tailored specifically to epitaphs, overcoming traditional research paths and systems of digitisation. Method. Based on the Chinese epitaph database built by the Zhejiang University Library and some commercial epitaph databases, an epitaph generative dialogue large language model was constructed using Doubao as the base model through pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and other full process trainings. Analysis. This study used human evaluation, in which experts, researchers, or general users assessed the quality of model-generated outputs. The evaluation included the epitaphs of Cui Yi, Liu Yi, and Lihua in the Tang dynasty. Results. The model successfully performed intelligent interpretation of epitaphs, automatic information extraction, and other knowledge-based services, thereby providing new ideas for constructing an ancient literature corpus from excavated materials represented by epitaphs. Conclusion. A large-scale domain-specific foundational model tailored for library applications was successfully developed. The study offers innovative approaches for processing historical texts and suggests new directions for AI integration in library knowledge systems.

Artificial intelligence now sits at the heart of digital marketing. Firms rely on it for everything from personalized product recommendations and automated customer conversations to predictive analytics, dynamic pricing, and real-time campaign adjustments. Yet these same capabilities carry real risks. Data is collected in ways customers may not expect. Algorithms can reflect hidden biases. Automated messages can veer into manipulation. And when customers sense any of this, trust is the first thing to go .Drawing on Trust Theory, Privacy Calculus Theory, Stakeholder Theory, Signaling Theory, and the Resource-Based View, the chapter sets out a framework that connects responsible AI practices to customer trust, marketing outcomes, and financial outcomes. The core argument is simple but important: responsible AI is not mainly a technical or compliance matter. It is a cross-functional marketing and financial capability that allows firms to build lasting customer relationships in markets where data is everywhere and trust is harder to earn than ever.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRAK: Pengintegrasian teknologi digital dalam proses pengajaran dan pembelajaran (PdP) Bahasa Melayu semakin diberi perhatian selaras dengan perkembangan pendidikan abad ke-21 dan transformasi pendidikan digital negara. Walau bagaimanapun, guru Bahasa Melayu masih berhadapan dengan pelbagai cabaran dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital secara berkesan semasa PdP. Oleh itu, kajian ini bertujuan untuk mengenal pasti jenis teknologi digital yang digunakan oleh guru Bahasa Melayu, meneliti cabaran yang dihadapi dalam mengaplikasikan teknologi digital serta menghuraikan cara guru mengatasi cabaran tersebut. Kajian ini menggunakan pendekatan Sorotan Literatur Sistematik (Systematic Literature Review, SLR) berpandukan garis panduan PRISMA. Sebanyak 15 artikel jurnal yang diterbitkan antara tahun 2021 hingga 2025 dan memenuhi kriteria inklusi telah dipilih serta dianalisis secara tematik. Dapatan kajian menunjukkan bahawa platform pembelajaran digital, aplikasi kolaboratif dan produktiviti digital, multimedia digital, aplikasi gamifikasi serta media sosial dan komunikasi digital merupakan teknologi yang dominan digunakan dalam PdP Bahasa Melayu. Cabaran utama yang dihadapi guru ialah kesukaran mengintegrasikan teknologi digital dalam PdP, kekurangan pengetahuan dan kemahiran digital, kekangan internet dan kemudahan teknologi, kekangan teknikal dan penyediaan bahan digital, penglibatan serta kesediaan murid, dan cabaran penggunaan teknologi baharu seperti kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence-AI). Bagi mengatasi cabaran tersebut, guru mengaplikasikan pelbagai strategi seperti memperkukuh latihan dan kolaborasi profesional, meningkatkan kompetensi digital, melaksanakan PdP yang interaktif dan berpusatkan murid, menambah baik akses teknologi serta memanfaatkan gamifikasi dan multimedia digital. Kajian ini memberikan implikasi bahawa pembangunan kompetensi digital guru dan penyediaan infrastruktur teknologi yang mencukupi perlu diperkukuh bagi memastikan keberkesanan pengintegrasian teknologi digital dalam PdP Bahasa Melayu.Kata kunci: Teknologi Digital, Guru Bahasa Melayu, Pengajaran dan Pembelajaran, Sorotan Literatur Sistematik, Pendidikan DigitalABSTRACT: The integration of digital technology in Malay language teaching and learning has gained increasing attention in line with the advancement of 21st-century education and the national digital education transformation agenda. Nevertheless, Malay language teachers continue to face various challenges in effectively implementing digital technology during the teaching and learning process. Therefore, this study aims to identify the types of digital technologies used by Malay language teachers, examine the challenges encountered in integrating digital technology, and explore the strategies employed to overcome these challenges. This study adopted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach guided by the PRISMA framework. A total of 15 journal articles published between 2021 and 2025 that met the inclusion criteria were selected and analysed thematically. The findings revealed that digital learning platforms, collaborative and productivity applications, digital multimedia, gamification applications, and social media and digital communication tools were among the most frequently used technologies in Malay language teaching and learning. The major challenges identified include difficulties in integrating digital technology into teaching practices, limited digital knowledge and skills among teachers, inadequate internet access and technological facilities, technical issues and digital material preparation, student engagement and readiness, as well as challenges associated with emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI). To address these challenges, teachers employed various strategies, including strengthening professional training and collaboration, enhancing digital competencies, implementing interactive and student-centred teaching approaches, improving access to technological resources, and utilising gamification and digital multimedia. The study implies that continuous development of teachers’ digital competencies and adequate technological infrastructure are essential to ensure the effective integration of digital technology in Malay language teaching and learning.Keywords: Digital Technology, Malay Language Teachers, Teaching and Learning, Systematic LiteratureReview, Digital Education

Purpose: To compare the internal consistency and convergent validity of the Short Form-36 (SF-36) and Short Form-12 (SF-12) questionnaires in patients with work-related musculoskeletal injuries. Methodological design: A quantitative, observational, analytical, and cross-sectional study was conducted using a non-probabilistic sample of 40 workers aged 18 to 65 years who received care at a secondary-level hospital in Irapuato, Guanajuato. Responses to the SF-12 items were extracted directly from the administered SF-36 questionnaires. The psychometric properties of both instruments were assessed through internal consistency, estimated using Cronbach’s alpha, and convergent validity, evaluated using Pearson’s correlation coefficient for the Physical Component Summary (PCS) and Mental Component Summary (MCS) scores. Results: Overall internal consistency was excellent for the SF-36 (α = 0.930) and good for the SF-12 (α = 0.803). Convergent validity analysis showed very strong, positive, and statistically significant correlations between the two versions for both the PCS (r = 0.981, p < 0.001) and the MCS (r = 0.956, p < 0.001). Research limitations: The cross-sectional design, small sample size, and concentration of participants in a single healthcare facility limit the generalizability of the findings. Further probabilistic, multicenter studies with larger samples are needed. Findings: Both instruments demonstrated adequate indicators of internal consistency and convergent validity in the study sample. The results support the use of the SF-12 as a shorter alternative for assessing health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in Occupational Health and Rehabilitation settings where time constraints are present.
topics: Health Systems, Economic Evaluations, Quality of Life

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly forms the operating logic of Indian urban governance, embedded in command-and-control centres, adaptive traffic systems, surveillance networks, and algorithmically mediated services. Yet smart-city scholarship evaluates such systems against managerial efficiency, leaving unexamined whether AI-enabled governance advances or erodes the constitutional guarantees underpinning public authority. This paper develops the Human-Centred Constitutional Urban AI Governance Framework and operationalises it as the Constitutional Smart-City Governance Index (CSGI), scoring urban AI against Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, human-centred AI principles, and Sustainable Development Goals 11 and 16. Six pillars constitutional rights, human-centred AI, sustainable development, service delivery, participation, and accountability comprise thirty-eight indicators with operational definitions, official secondary-data sources, a transparent normalisation-and-weighting model, and a validation strategy. The CSGI is applied to four leading smart cities Bengaluru, Pune, Surat, and Indore through a governance-opacity audit, an index-divergence analysis, and a Monte Carlo robustness test. The cities are 86%–93% opaque; none publishes an algorithm register, data-protection impact assessment, independent algorithmic audit, or municipal AI policy. The CSGI correlates strongly negatively with the Ease of Living Index (Spearman ρ = −0.80) yet positively with municipal-performance and sanitation indices ( ρ = +0.80 to + 0.95), revealing a constitutional blind spot in liveability metrics steering national policy. Across 20,000 sampled weight vectors, the lowest-ranked city is weight-invariant. Because comparable cross-city data remain sparse, the application is illustrative rather than validated itself a finding. The paper contributes a transferable, reproducible instrument, repositions constitutional law as urban-governance infrastructure, and offers tiered recommendations for national, state, and local authorities.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in judicial systems raises a fundamental question under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR): can an AI system genuinely fulfil a litigant’s right to be heard? This article develops a functional account of that right as a multifaceted guarantee requiring the opportunity to present and challenge relevant material, effective examination of decisive submissions, clarification where necessary, contextual and normative evaluation, reasoned decision-making, and responsibility for the outcome. Using doctrinal, comparative, and normative methods, the study examines these requirements in relation to risks associated with judicial AI, including opacity, algorithmic bias, hallucinated outputs, limited explainability, and automation bias. The analysis is situated within the EU AI Act, the GDPR, the CEPEJ Ethical Charter, Romanian civil procedure, and comparative administrative-law cases. The article finds that AI may legitimately assist courts through transcription, translation, legal research, document organization, and non-binding summaries or drafts. However, under current legal and technological conditions, AI cannot autonomously perform the hearing in its entirety. Compliance with Article 6 therefore requires transparency, contestability, independent judicial verification, and meaningful human oversight. Final adjudicative authority, reasoned judgment, and responsibility must remain with an independent and accountable human judge.

documents.abstract: Recent advances in AI make Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) increasingly plausible. Large Language Models (LLMs) can already propose, select, and run Machine Learning (ML) experiments. However, the space of possible design choices in ML is vast. An LLM that proposes an experiment needs a reliable intuition of whether it is worth running given the timing constraints of long training runs. In this work, we measure such intuition in current frontier LLMs by evaluating how accurately they predict the impact of self-generated ML experiment ideas before these are put into training runs. To this end, we construct a dataset of 288 LLM-proposed ideas on eight MLE-bench tasks. We then prompt five frontier LLMs (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3) to predict the impact of each idea and compare their predictions with the actual outcomes after training. We report four main findings. First, LLM predictions are substantially better than random chance but far from accurate: even the best model, Claude Opus 5.5, explains only half of the variance in outcomes (R^2 = 0.49). Second, we notice that all tested models systematically underestimate the magnitude of the changes. Third, prediction quality varies widely across tasks. Finally, the choice of the coding harness that actually implements the ideas has little effect on outcomes, and we find no evidence of self-preference. Higher reasoning settings and additional context lead to modest gains. Overall, our results show that current LLMs have useful but limited intuition about which ML ideas will work. We release our dataset to support further study.

Every story has two orders: the order in which its events happen and the order in which they are told. A story is nonlinear when the two differ. We introduce a benchmark of 83 published works that measures whether language models can tell nonlinear stories. For each work, we annotate one list of events in both orders, together with a story graph of causal dependencies, character knowledge, and the questions the telling raises and resolves. Given events in chronological order, all 19 models tell them, on average, more chronologically than the published works do; asked for a specific structure, they land within the human range about half the time. We then compare a model's stories of the same events under different conditions, using both an automated judge and 71 human readers. Both prefer the chronological story a model writes by default to the nonlinear one it writes on request, which readers find harder to follow in 81% of decisive judgments. Readers also prefer stories written from the story graph to stories constrained to the published telling order (72% of decisive judgments), a difference the judge does not detect. Our results suggest that following an instruction to reorder a story is not yet the same as telling it well out of order.

Purpose This paper explores the effects of artificial intelligence (AI) on university teaching in sport management subjects. It investigates how AI-driven tools, such as ChatGPT, Copilot, and other generative systems, are reshaping pedagogical models, fostering innovation in curriculum design, and enhancing the personalization of learning experiences within higher education institutions. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design was adopted, involving semi-structured interviews with 17 professors from eight European universities offering sport management programs. Data were analyzed using thematic content analysis with AI-assisted coding through MAXQDA software to identify key dimensions of educational transformation, faculty perceptions, and ethical concerns. Findings Results reveal that AI enhances personalized learning, supports data-informed decision-making, and facilitates real-time feedback in sport management education. Educators view AI as a valuable tool for simulating real-world scenarios, optimizing resource management, and improving student engagement and creativity. However, persistent concerns emerge regarding ethical governance, data privacy, and the potential over-reliance on AI-generated content. The study emphasizes the urgent need to strengthen AI literacy, ethical awareness, and institutional guidelines for responsible adoption. Originality/value This research is among the first to examine AI integration in sport management education from a European academic perspective. It contributes by linking theoretical insights on AI pedagogy with practical applications, highlighting the ethical and professional implications of emerging technologies in a digitally transforming field.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is reshaping how students access, produce, verify, and communicate information, raising questions about source authority, adab, values, and character formation in Islamic Religious Education (IRE). This study examines the challenges facing IRE teachers and proposes a repositioning of their roles from an Islamic epistemological perspective. A qualitative library research approach was employed, drawing on literature on Islamic education and epistemology, teacher ethics, UNESCO guidance on AI in education, and recent studies on AI and IRE. Sources were examined through content and conceptual analysis. The findings position AI as a supporting instrument subject to human epistemic oversight and identify teachers’ roles as knowledge curators, information validators, digital ethics mentors, learning designers, and exemplars of adab. AI outputs should be evaluated within the relationship among revelation, reason, experience, scholarly tradition, and technology. The study proposes the IRE teacher as an epistemic gatekeeper responsible for safeguarding information quality, guiding verification, and aligning technology use with Islamic educational aims. To support implementation, it introduces the Verifikasi model, comprising source verification, ethical use, reflection, integration of religious evidence, process orientation, human initiative, and accountability. The study contributes a conceptual basis and an implementation model for repositioning IRE teachers, emphasizing that AI integration should strengthen literacy, critical reasoning, and adab while preserving human responsibility in education.

We study personalized LLM routing, where a router selects among heterogeneous models with different costs and capabilities. The router must minimize cumulative inference cost while ensuring reliable realized response quality, even though user preferences are unknown and must be learned from feedback during deployment. We formulate this problem as a constrained contextual bandit and develop an algorithm that learns preferences while balancing cost and quality. Under a logistic preference model and a strict-feasibility condition, we establish sublinear expected cost regret relative to an optimal stationary randomized contextual oracle and a high-probability guarantee on realized cumulative satisfaction. The framework extends beyond LLM routing to broader online model-selection problems with reliability requirements.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychological constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understudied. To address this gap, we define and systematically investigate scale sensitivity, the variation in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sensitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpretation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alternative scales.

Aims This study investigated changes in activity patterns, cognitive functions, and fatigue following activity management training in individuals with chronic low back pain (CLBP).Patients and methods Thirty-four individuals with CLBP completed a six-week training program covering ergonomics, pacing, energy conservation, and relaxation. Assessments included the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM), Body Awareness Questionnaire, Patterns of Activity Measure-Pain, Cognitive Failures Questionnaire (CFQ), Fatigue Severity Scale, Stroop Test, and selected Loewenstein Occupational Therapy Cognitive Assessment (LOTCA) subtests.Results Significant improvements were observed in COPM performance and satisfaction (p < 0.001). Body awareness and adaptive activity regulation behaviors increased, while pain-related avoidance behaviors decreased (p < 0.05). Cognitive performance also improved, as indicated by lower CFQ scores and better performance on selected Stroop and LOTCA measures (p < 0.05). Fatigue severity did not change significantly (p > 0.05). Regression models were significant for activity performance (R2 = 0.366, p = 0.008) and satisfaction (R2 = 0.347, p = 0.013). Body awareness and visuomotor organization were associated with activity performance, while fatigue was associated with activity satisfaction (p < 0.05). Conclusions Activity management training may be considered a supportive approach for addressing activity-related difficulties in individuals with chronic low back pain.ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier www.clinicaltrials.gov identifier is NCT07061743.
